380	## 2. Cross-cutting synthesis
381	
382	### (a) The common step sequence in modern infra purchase flows
383	The convergent shape across DigitalOcean, Hetzner and Vultr is:
384	
385	1. **WHERE** — region/location (defaulted or recommended)
386	2. **WHAT SIZE** — plan family → specific plan (the price-determining choice)
387	3. **WHAT ON IT** — image: OS *or* one-click app/marketplace *or* snapshot (tabs at one decision point)
388	4. **HOW DO I GET IN** — auth: SSH key (recommended) vs password
389	5. **EXTRAS** — backups, networking, firewall, monitoring, user-data (all optional, all grouped)
390	6. **IDENTITY** — hostname/label, tags, project (mostly optional)
391	7. **COMMIT** — create/deploy/buy → provisioning progress → connection details
392	
393	Divergence by product type:
394	- **Compute:** as above. Payment is account-level and implicit; the create button *is* the purchase.
395	- **Domain:** search → availability → **term** → registrant contact set → payment → near-instant completion
396	  (Cloudflare: "up to 30 seconds"). Uniquely, the *legal* fields (contacts) are mandatory pre-payment because the
397	  registry requires them. Everything else in the category can be deferred.
398	- **Email:** purchase seats → **then** a multi-day, externally-dependent setup (verify domain → MX → SPF/DKIM/DMARC →
399	  create mailboxes). The valuable UX work is entirely post-payment, and it is stateful and resumable.
400	- **Game:** plan (by RAM/players) → term → payment → **then** game/software/modpack selection via one-click installer
401	  → panel. The technical choice is deliberately post-payment (Shockbyte). Free tier inverts it further: no payment at
402	  all, create → queue → run, with the upgrade path introduced only when a limit bites.
403	- **Shared hosting:** plan → term → payment → then domain attach (register new / use existing) → then site install
404	  (one-click app or builder). Two clean post-payment stages.
405	
406	### (b) Fields asked pre-payment, per competitor per product type
407	
408	| Company | Product | Asked BEFORE the commit action | Deferred to after |
409	|---|---|---|---|
410	| DigitalOcean | Compute | region, size, image, auth method, hostname | project, tags, monitoring agent config, firewall rules |
411	| Hetzner | Compute | type, location, image, IP config, name (+ SSH key strongly encouraged) | volumes, firewall, backups can be added later; SSH key **cannot** |
412	| Vultr | Compute | type, location, plan, image, hostname + label | SSH keys, startup script, firewall group, backups, DDoS (all optional at deploy) |
413	| Vercel | PaaS | repo, team, project name | env vars, build settings (pre-filled), domain |
414	| Railway | PaaS | repo/image/template + required template inputs | variables, domain, scaling |
415	| Cloudflare Registrar | Domain | domain, term, 4 contact roles, payment method, agreement | DNS records, WHOIS prefs, nameservers |
416	| Porkbun | Domain | domain, term, contacts, payment | DNS, forwarding, SSL (all included, configured later) |
417	| Namecheap [MEMORY] | Domain | domain, term, contacts, add-on checkboxes, payment | DNS, hosting |
418	| Google Workspace | Email | plan, seat count, admin identity, payment | **domain verification, MX, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, mailbox creation** |
419	| Shockbyte | Game | plan (RAM), billing cycle, location, payment | server software/modpack, version, config, whitelist |
420	| Apex | Game | plan (RAM), term, payment | game/modpack, version, all config |
421	| Aternos | Free game | account only (email optional) | everything: software, version, options, mods |
422	| Hostinger | VPS | plan, term, region, payment | **hostname, root password, SSH key, OS finalisation** |
423	
424	Reading of the table: **the only fields that genuinely must precede payment are the ones that determine the price
425	(plan, term, region, quantity) and the ones a third party legally requires (registrant contacts).** Every competitor
426	that sells to non-experts defers the rest.
427	
428	### (c) Two-stage checkout → post-payment setup
429	
430	Who already does it: **Hostinger** (VPS hostname/root password/SSH after payment, ending in "Finish setup"),
431	**Shockbyte and Apex** (game software/modpack chosen post-purchase via one-click installer),
432	**Google Workspace** (the entire DNS/email setup is post-payment and multi-day),
433	**Vercel/Railway** (deploy first, then domain and env vars),
434	**Cloudflare add-site** (plan chosen at the start, but records and nameservers are a separate post-onboarding stage).
435	
436	Principles for the model:
437	1. **Stage 1 asks only price-determining and legally-required inputs.** If a field does not change the amount charged
438	   and is not required by a registry/registrar, it belongs in stage 2.
439	2. **The transition must be explicit and reassuring** — payment confirmation should immediately name what happens
440	   next and roughly how long it takes, not dump the user on a generic dashboard.
441	3. **Stage 2 must be resumable and idempotent.** The user may close the tab, pay on mobile and configure on desktop,
442	   or hand it to a colleague. Persist a setup record server-side; never hold it in form state.
443	4. **Stage 2 must be skippable with safe defaults**, and the skipped items must reappear as a persistent task
444	   (Google's standing "Set up Admin Console" prompt is the reference behaviour).
445	5. **Stage 2 ends with a review-and-confirm**, because it is the last point before an irreversible provision
446	   (Hostinger's "Finish setup").
447	6. **Never let stage 2 silently create a half-provisioned resource the user is billed for** — if setup is abandoned,
448	   the resource's state must say so plainly on the dashboard.
449	7. **One-time secrets belong at the end of stage 2, shown once, with an explicit "you will not see this again"**
450	   (Hetzner's root password behaviour), plus a documented rotation path.
451	
452	### (d) IA models compared
453	
454	| Model | Who | Pros | Cons for a multi-product host |
455	|---|---|---|---|
456	| **Product-centric** (nav = catalogue: Compute, Storage, Domains, Email…) | Vultr; Cloudflare's dashboard largely | Matches how the company builds and bills; easy to add a product; a new customer with one product sees a short list | Fragments a single customer's *website* across 4 sections; the nav grows with the catalogue, not with the customer's usage; forces the user to know which product a task lives in |
457	| **Project-centric** (nav = user's groupings, resources hang off them) | DigitalOcean (soft), Hetzner (hard), Vercel, Railway | Groups heterogeneous resources by the thing the customer actually cares about; scales to agencies/resellers; natural home for per-site billing views | Overhead for the 1-VPS customer; hard scoping (Hetzner) makes cross-project search and global views poor; requires a good default project or it becomes a blocker |
458	| **Task-centric** (nav = jobs: "Connect a domain", "Set up email", "Install an app") | Google Workspace setup; Cloudflare add-site onboarding; Hostinger's onboarding stage | Best possible first-run experience; matches novice mental models; makes multi-product cross-sell feel like help rather than upsell | Does not scale as a permanent nav — power users need direct object access; task lists go stale; ambiguous where a *thing* lives once its task is done |
459	
460	**Recommendation for Nxeon:** a hybrid. Resource-list home (flat, all products, one searchable inventory) +
461	**optional** project/site grouping with a default bucket (DigitalOcean's pattern, not Hetzner's) + a **task-centric
462	overlay** for onboarding and any incomplete setup (Google's standing-task pattern). Global search must span *all*
463	products and resource attributes (IP, domain, server name, ticket, invoice) — Hetzner's per-project scoping is the
464	thing to avoid for a host whose customers buy across categories.
465	
466	### (e) Provisioning-progress honesty
467	
468	Who shows real state:
469	- **Vercel/Railway** — genuinely real: streamed build logs plus named deployment states. Vercel's own docs concede
470	  logs are hard to read, which is the argument for a stage model *on top of* logs.
471	- **Aternos** — real and remarkable: queue *position* and ETA, plus a liveness confirmation, plus a visible countdown
472	  before auto-shutdown. It exposes a scarcity constraint rather than concealing it.
473	- **DigitalOcean** — a real progress bar tied to provisioning, then the IP appears.
474	- **Cloudflare add-site** — honest about tooling limits: the DNS scan "is not guaranteed to find all existing records".
475	- **Google Workspace** — honest about *time*: ~10 min to add, ~1 hr to confirm, with consequences dated.
476	
477	Who leans on theatre: much of the "Instant Setup" marketing in the game-host category, and any spinner-with-fake-steps
478	pattern where the backend only knows queued/running/done.
479	
480	**How to be honest when the backend reports only coarse states** — the practical pattern for Nxeon:
481	1. **Model stages, not percentages.** Name 3–5 real stages (Queued → Allocating → Installing OS → Booting → Ready).
482	   Each stage is a real backend state or a real substep; do not interpolate a fake percentage between them.
483	2. **Show elapsed time, and a p50/p90 expectation** ("usually 2–4 minutes"), not a countdown you cannot honour.
484	3. **Distinguish "still working" from "stuck".** Past the p90, change the message to say so and offer an action
485	   (check status, contact support) — never keep spinning silently.
486	4. **Never advance a stage the backend has not reported.** If the backend only knows queued/running/done, show three
487	   stages, not eight.
488	5. **Explain the wait's cause where you can** (capacity queue, image download, DNS propagation). Aternos proves that
489	   an explained wait is tolerated far better than an unexplained one.
490	6. **Make the page survivable** — refreshable, linkable, emailed. Provisioning must not depend on a live tab.
491	7. **Deliver first value the moment it exists**, not at the end: show the IP/connection details as soon as they are
492	   assigned, marked as "not ready yet" until boot completes.
493	
494	### (f) Domain-search UX principles
495	1. Search must work **before signup** (guest search + cart; Namecheap [MEMORY]); account creation belongs at checkout.
496	2. Show **registration / renewal / transfer prices together** at result time (Porkbun's three-column TLD table). This
497	   is the single highest-trust intervention in the category.
498	3. Never dead-end an unavailable name: offer alternative TLDs and near-miss variants. Porkbun's own weakness is
499	   exactly this (no as-you-type results, no generated suggestions).
500	4. State what is **included** rather than selling it: WHOIS privacy, DNSSEC, SSL, forwarding (Cloudflare and Porkbun
501	   both bundle by default and say so).
502	5. **No upsell checkboxes in checkout.** Offer complements after the domain is secured.
503	6. Ask the registrant contact set **once**, copy it across required roles, and save it as a reusable profile — do not
504	   present four contact roles as four forms (Cloudflare's flow is the cautionary case).
505	7. Auto-renew on by default, clearly stated and one click to disable, with a dated renewal reminder policy.
506	8. Confirm fast and concretely — a stated processing expectation ("up to 30 seconds") beats an open-ended spinner.
507	9. Immediately after purchase, name the **one next action** (point it at a Nxeon service, or set nameservers).
508	
509	### (g) Email setup + DNS verification UX principles
510	1. Treat setup as a **persistent, resumable checklist with a status per step**, not a wizard that can be lost
511	   (Google: per-domain status column + standing "set up" prompt).
512	2. Give every DNS record in **copy-ready form** (host, type, value, TTL) with one-click copy, and show the *exact*
513	   value rather than a template.
514	3. **Detect the registrar/nameserver and give specific instructions**, with a generic fallback — Google does exactly
515	   this for popular registrars. When Nxeon *is* the registrar or DNS host, offer a one-click "add these records for
516	   me", which converts the hardest step into a button.
517	4. **State realistic propagation windows** and consequences with dates.
518	5. Verification must be **diagnostic**: on failure, show what was queried, what was found, and what was expected.
519	   A bare "verification failed" is the category's worst pattern.
520	6. Cover the full record set explicitly and group by purpose — MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC (Cloudflare groups email records
521	   as their own bucket during import). Nxeon's own DKIM incident is evidence that the *authoritative* source must be
522	   queried, not a local resolver.
523	7. Warn before destructive DNS changes — Cloudflare's onboarding both scans existing records and warns that DNSSEC
524	   must be disabled before a nameserver change. Any flow that replaces nameservers must show what will stop working.
525	8. Re-check automatically on a schedule after the user says "I've added it", and notify on success — do not make the
526	   user poll.
527	
528	### (h) Game-server picker principles
529	1. **Categorise by game first**, then by scale. Game identity is the primary filter for this audience.
530	2. **Ask the buyer's language, answer in yours.** Take "how many players?" and "vanilla / plugins / modpack?" as
531	   inputs and *output* a recommended plan. Apex has exactly this mapping (2 GB ≈ 10 players vanilla, 4 GB ≈ 40-mod
532	   pack, 8–10 GB large modpacks/communities) but leaves it in a guide article instead of the picker.
533	3. **Recommend explicitly** — one highlighted plan plus use-case badges ("most popular", "good for modpacks") beats a
534	   grid of specs (Shockbyte's badge approach, minus the RAM-only tiering).
535	4. **De-risk the choice in the picker itself**: "change plan any time" (Apex allows up/downgrade) removes the fear of
536	   picking wrong, which is the main hesitation for a first-time buyer.
537	5. **Signal mod support honestly.** Say precisely what exists — file/SFTP access, a modpack installer, or neither.
538	   Nxeon already established this honest line on the mods page and must not let the picker overclaim.
539	6. **Defer software/version/modpack to post-purchase** with a one-click installer (Shockbyte, Aternos).
540	7. **Free-tier → paid path:** surface the limit *at the moment it bites*, framed as a fact plus an option — during a
541	   queue wait, at the auto-sleep countdown, at a RAM/storage ceiling, at a player-count cap. Never a generic banner.
542	   The upgrade must **carry the world/config across**, and that continuity must be promised in the prompt; the fear of
543	   losing the world is the real blocker, not price.
544	8. **Keep the panel vocabulary standard** (Console, Files, Backups, Players, Settings, Startup/Network) so users
545	   arriving from a Pterodactyl-based host are instantly oriented.
546	9. **Name power actions honestly**, including a Kill that is described as a last resort.
547	
548	### (i) Pricing transparency principles
549	1. **Show the renewal/recurring price next to the promotional price, at equal prominence.** Cloudflare (renewal =
550	   registry list price) and Porkbun (register ≈ renew) both make this the selling point.
551	2. **Hourly rate + monthly cap together** for anything metered (Hetzner). State that the bill cannot exceed the cap.
552	3. **State what still bills when a resource is stopped** (Hetzner: a powered-off server still bills for disk and IP).
553	   Failing to say this is a top source of billing disputes.
554	4. **Price add-ons as visible deltas** (backups +$X/mo, DDoS +$Y/mo) rather than folding them into a total.
555	5. **Show a running configuration total** that updates as choices change, plus a final line-item summary before commit.
556	6. **Tax/VAT/GST:** show it as a named line before the commit action, with the jurisdiction basis, and honour the
557	   local convention for the customer's region. Never let the charged amount exceed the last figure shown.
558	7. **Currency:** display in the customer's currency where possible but state the billing currency explicitly if it
559	   differs, since the card statement will show the billing currency.
560	8. **No add-ons injected into checkout.** Offer complements before or after, never at the payment step.
561	9. **Bundle-and-say-so** beats sell-and-upsell for commodity extras (WHOIS privacy, SSL, DNS, forwarding).
562	10. **Term discounts must show both numbers** — the discounted term rate and the rate after it.
563	
564	### (j) 12 concrete UX principles Nxeon should adopt
565	
566	1. **Split every purchase into stage 1 (price-determining fields + payment) and stage 2 (a resumable post-payment
567	   setup wizard).** WHY: it shortens the path to the money step and moves the intimidating technical decisions to
568	   after commitment, where the customer is motivated and can be guided. EVIDENCE: Hostinger collects hostname/root
569	   password/SSH after payment ending in "Finish setup" (hostinger.com/tutorials/how-to-set-up-vps); Shockbyte defers
570	   server software to a post-purchase installer (shockbyte.com/minecraft).
571	2. **Ask before payment only what changes the price or is legally required.** WHY: every optional pre-payment field is
572	   a drop-off point. EVIDENCE: the pre-payment column in (b) — no competitor asks for optional config before the
573	   commit except Hetzner, whose flow is the longest in the set.
574	3. **Auto-detect and pre-fill anything inferable; show it as editable rather than asking.** WHY: turns required
575	   decisions into confirmations. EVIDENCE: Vercel auto-detects framework and build settings and allows
576	   "Deploy Now" without touching them (vercel.com/docs/getting-started-with-vercel).
577	4. **Chunk long configuration into 2–3 named stages with explicit advance actions.** WHY: reduces perceived length
578	   without removing control. EVIDENCE: Vultr's "Configure Software" / "Server Settings" / "Additional Features"
579	   staging (docs.vultr.com/products/compute/instances/cloud-compute/provisioning).
580	5. **Model provisioning as named real stages with elapsed time and a p50/p90 expectation; never fake a percentage.**
581	   WHY: honesty survives the inevitable slow provision; theatre does not. EVIDENCE: Aternos shows queue position and
582	   ETA; Google states ~10 min / ~1 hr expectations; Cloudflare admits its DNS scan may be incomplete.
583	6. **Explain any wait's cause, and confirm liveness before consuming scarce capacity.** WHY: an explained wait is
584	   tolerated; an unexplained one is abandonment. EVIDENCE: Aternos' queue position + ETA + green confirmation step
585	   before start (support.aternos.org/hc/en-us/articles/360026950812-Queue).
586	7. **Show registration / renewal / transfer prices side by side at domain-search time, and hourly + monthly cap on
587	   every compute plan.** WHY: renewal shock and billing surprise are the two biggest trust failures in this industry.
588	   EVIDENCE: Porkbun's three-column TLD pricing; Cloudflare's at-cost renewal policy
589	   (developers.cloudflare.com/registrar/); Hetzner's hourly-rate-with-monthly-cap model.
590	8. **Bundle commodity extras and say they are included; put zero upsells in checkout.** WHY: it differentiates on
591	   trust, which is Nxeon's competitive lever as an owner-operated host. EVIDENCE: Porkbun bundles WHOIS privacy, SSL,
592	   forwarding with no checkout upsells; Cloudflare includes WHOIS redaction and DNSSEC.
593	9. **Turn every incomplete setup into a persistent, resumable task with a visible status — never a modal.** WHY:
594	   multi-day, externally-dependent setup (DNS, email) cannot live in form state. EVIDENCE: Google Workspace's
595	   per-domain status column plus standing "Set up Admin Console" prompt.
596	10. **Make DNS/email verification diagnostic: show queried vs expected, offer registrar-specific steps, and one-click
597	    "add these records for me" when Nxeon controls the zone.** WHY: turns the hardest step into a button and makes
598	    failures self-serviceable. EVIDENCE: Google's registrar-specific instructions with a generic fallback; Cloudflare's
599	    grouped record review during add-site.

## 2. Cross-cutting synthesis

### (a) The common step sequence in modern infra purchase flows
The convergent shape across DigitalOcean, Hetzner and Vultr is:

1. **WHERE** — region/location (defaulted or recommended)
2. **WHAT SIZE** — plan family → specific plan (the price-determining choice)
3. **WHAT ON IT** — image: OS *or* one-click app/marketplace *or* snapshot (tabs at one decision point)
4. **HOW DO I GET IN** — auth: SSH key (recommended) vs password
5. **EXTRAS** — backups, networking, firewall, monitoring, user-data (all optional, all grouped)
6. **IDENTITY** — hostname/label, tags, project (mostly optional)
7. **COMMIT** — create/deploy/buy → provisioning progress → connection details

Divergence by product type:
- **Compute:** as above. Payment is account-level and implicit; the create button *is* the purchase.
- **Domain:** search → availability → **term** → registrant contact set → payment → near-instant completion
  (Cloudflare: "up to 30 seconds"). Uniquely, the *legal* fields (contacts) are mandatory pre-payment because the
  registry requires them. Everything else in the category can be deferred.
- **Email:** purchase seats → **then** a multi-day, externally-dependent setup (verify domain → MX → SPF/DKIM/DMARC →
  create mailboxes). The valuable UX work is entirely post-payment, and it is stateful and resumable.
- **Game:** plan (by RAM/players) → term → payment → **then** game/software/modpack selection via one-click installer
  → panel. The technical choice is deliberately post-payment (Shockbyte). Free tier inverts it further: no payment at
  all, create → queue → run, with the upgrade path introduced only when a limit bites.
- **Shared hosting:** plan → term → payment → then domain attach (register new / use existing) → then site install
  (one-click app or builder). Two clean post-payment stages.

### (b) Fields asked pre-payment, per competitor per product type

| Company | Product | Asked BEFORE the commit action | Deferred to after |
|---|---|---|---|
| DigitalOcean | Compute | region, size, image, auth method, hostname | project, tags, monitoring agent config, firewall rules |
| Hetzner | Compute | type, location, image, IP config, name (+ SSH key strongly encouraged) | volumes, firewall, backups can be added later; SSH key **cannot** |
| Vultr | Compute | type, location, plan, image, hostname + label | SSH keys, startup script, firewall group, backups, DDoS (all optional at deploy) |
| Vercel | PaaS | repo, team, project name | env vars, build settings (pre-filled), domain |
| Railway | PaaS | repo/image/template + required template inputs | variables, domain, scaling |
| Cloudflare Registrar | Domain | domain, term, 4 contact roles, payment method, agreement | DNS records, WHOIS prefs, nameservers |
| Porkbun | Domain | domain, term, contacts, payment | DNS, forwarding, SSL (all included, configured later) |
| Namecheap [MEMORY] | Domain | domain, term, contacts, add-on checkboxes, payment | DNS, hosting |
| Google Workspace | Email | plan, seat count, admin identity, payment | **domain verification, MX, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, mailbox creation** |
| Shockbyte | Game | plan (RAM), billing cycle, location, payment | server software/modpack, version, config, whitelist |
| Apex | Game | plan (RAM), term, payment | game/modpack, version, all config |
| Aternos | Free game | account only (email optional) | everything: software, version, options, mods |
| Hostinger | VPS | plan, term, region, payment | **hostname, root password, SSH key, OS finalisation** |

Reading of the table: **the only fields that genuinely must precede payment are the ones that determine the price
(plan, term, region, quantity) and the ones a third party legally requires (registrant contacts).** Every competitor
that sells to non-experts defers the rest.

### (c) Two-stage checkout → post-payment setup

Who already does it: **Hostinger** (VPS hostname/root password/SSH after payment, ending in "Finish setup"),
**Shockbyte and Apex** (game software/modpack chosen post-purchase via one-click installer),
**Google Workspace** (the entire DNS/email setup is post-payment and multi-day),
**Vercel/Railway** (deploy first, then domain and env vars),
**Cloudflare add-site** (plan chosen at the start, but records and nameservers are a separate post-onboarding stage).

Principles for the model:
1. **Stage 1 asks only price-determining and legally-required inputs.** If a field does not change the amount charged
   and is not required by a registry/registrar, it belongs in stage 2.
2. **The transition must be explicit and reassuring** — payment confirmation should immediately name what happens
   next and roughly how long it takes, not dump the user on a generic dashboard.
3. **Stage 2 must be resumable and idempotent.** The user may close the tab, pay on mobile and configure on desktop,
   or hand it to a colleague. Persist a setup record server-side; never hold it in form state.
4. **Stage 2 must be skippable with safe defaults**, and the skipped items must reappear as a persistent task
   (Google's standing "Set up Admin Console" prompt is the reference behaviour).
5. **Stage 2 ends with a review-and-confirm**, because it is the last point before an irreversible provision
   (Hostinger's "Finish setup").
6. **Never let stage 2 silently create a half-provisioned resource the user is billed for** — if setup is abandoned,
   the resource's state must say so plainly on the dashboard.
7. **One-time secrets belong at the end of stage 2, shown once, with an explicit "you will not see this again"**
   (Hetzner's root password behaviour), plus a documented rotation path.

### (d) IA models compared

| Model | Who | Pros | Cons for a multi-product host |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Product-centric** (nav = catalogue: Compute, Storage, Domains, Email…) | Vultr; Cloudflare's dashboard largely | Matches how the company builds and bills; easy to add a product; a new customer with one product sees a short list | Fragments a single customer's *website* across 4 sections; the nav grows with the catalogue, not with the customer's usage; forces the user to know which product a task lives in |
| **Project-centric** (nav = user's groupings, resources hang off them) | DigitalOcean (soft), Hetzner (hard), Vercel, Railway | Groups heterogeneous resources by the thing the customer actually cares about; scales to agencies/resellers; natural home for per-site billing views | Overhead for the 1-VPS customer; hard scoping (Hetzner) makes cross-project search and global views poor; requires a good default project or it becomes a blocker |
| **Task-centric** (nav = jobs: "Connect a domain", "Set up email", "Install an app") | Google Workspace setup; Cloudflare add-site onboarding; Hostinger's onboarding stage | Best possible first-run experience; matches novice mental models; makes multi-product cross-sell feel like help rather than upsell | Does not scale as a permanent nav — power users need direct object access; task lists go stale; ambiguous where a *thing* lives once its task is done |

**Recommendation for Nxeon:** a hybrid. Resource-list home (flat, all products, one searchable inventory) +
**optional** project/site grouping with a default bucket (DigitalOcean's pattern, not Hetzner's) + a **task-centric
overlay** for onboarding and any incomplete setup (Google's standing-task pattern). Global search must span *all*
products and resource attributes (IP, domain, server name, ticket, invoice) — Hetzner's per-project scoping is the
thing to avoid for a host whose customers buy across categories.

### (e) Provisioning-progress honesty

Who shows real state:
- **Vercel/Railway** — genuinely real: streamed build logs plus named deployment states. Vercel's own docs concede
  logs are hard to read, which is the argument for a stage model *on top of* logs.
- **Aternos** — real and remarkable: queue *position* and ETA, plus a liveness confirmation, plus a visible countdown
  before auto-shutdown. It exposes a scarcity constraint rather than concealing it.
- **DigitalOcean** — a real progress bar tied to provisioning, then the IP appears.
- **Cloudflare add-site** — honest about tooling limits: the DNS scan "is not guaranteed to find all existing records".
- **Google Workspace** — honest about *time*: ~10 min to add, ~1 hr to confirm, with consequences dated.

Who leans on theatre: much of the "Instant Setup" marketing in the game-host category, and any spinner-with-fake-steps
pattern where the backend only knows queued/running/done.

**How to be honest when the backend reports only coarse states** — the practical pattern for Nxeon:
1. **Model stages, not percentages.** Name 3–5 real stages (Queued → Allocating → Installing OS → Booting → Ready).
   Each stage is a real backend state or a real substep; do not interpolate a fake percentage between them.
2. **Show elapsed time, and a p50/p90 expectation** ("usually 2–4 minutes"), not a countdown you cannot honour.
3. **Distinguish "still working" from "stuck".** Past the p90, change the message to say so and offer an action
   (check status, contact support) — never keep spinning silently.
4. **Never advance a stage the backend has not reported.** If the backend only knows queued/running/done, show three
   stages, not eight.
5. **Explain the wait's cause where you can** (capacity queue, image download, DNS propagation). Aternos proves that
   an explained wait is tolerated far better than an unexplained one.
6. **Make the page survivable** — refreshable, linkable, emailed. Provisioning must not depend on a live tab.
7. **Deliver first value the moment it exists**, not at the end: show the IP/connection details as soon as they are
   assigned, marked as "not ready yet" until boot completes.

### (f) Domain-search UX principles
1. Search must work **before signup** (guest search + cart; Namecheap [MEMORY]); account creation belongs at checkout.
2. Show **registration / renewal / transfer prices together** at result time (Porkbun's three-column TLD table). This
   is the single highest-trust intervention in the category.
3. Never dead-end an unavailable name: offer alternative TLDs and near-miss variants. Porkbun's own weakness is
   exactly this (no as-you-type results, no generated suggestions).
4. State what is **included** rather than selling it: WHOIS privacy, DNSSEC, SSL, forwarding (Cloudflare and Porkbun
   both bundle by default and say so).
5. **No upsell checkboxes in checkout.** Offer complements after the domain is secured.
6. Ask the registrant contact set **once**, copy it across required roles, and save it as a reusable profile — do not
   present four contact roles as four forms (Cloudflare's flow is the cautionary case).
7. Auto-renew on by default, clearly stated and one click to disable, with a dated renewal reminder policy.
8. Confirm fast and concretely — a stated processing expectation ("up to 30 seconds") beats an open-ended spinner.
9. Immediately after purchase, name the **one next action** (point it at a Nxeon service, or set nameservers).

### (g) Email setup + DNS verification UX principles
1. Treat setup as a **persistent, resumable checklist with a status per step**, not a wizard that can be lost
   (Google: per-domain status column + standing "set up" prompt).
2. Give every DNS record in **copy-ready form** (host, type, value, TTL) with one-click copy, and show the *exact*
   value rather than a template.
3. **Detect the registrar/nameserver and give specific instructions**, with a generic fallback — Google does exactly
   this for popular registrars. When Nxeon *is* the registrar or DNS host, offer a one-click "add these records for
   me", which converts the hardest step into a button.
4. **State realistic propagation windows** and consequences with dates.
5. Verification must be **diagnostic**: on failure, show what was queried, what was found, and what was expected.
   A bare "verification failed" is the category's worst pattern.
6. Cover the full record set explicitly and group by purpose — MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC (Cloudflare groups email records
   as their own bucket during import). Nxeon's own DKIM incident is evidence that the *authoritative* source must be
   queried, not a local resolver.
7. Warn before destructive DNS changes — Cloudflare's onboarding both scans existing records and warns that DNSSEC
   must be disabled before a nameserver change. Any flow that replaces nameservers must show what will stop working.
8. Re-check automatically on a schedule after the user says "I've added it", and notify on success — do not make the
   user poll.

### (h) Game-server picker principles
1. **Categorise by game first**, then by scale. Game identity is the primary filter for this audience.
2. **Ask the buyer's language, answer in yours.** Take "how many players?" and "vanilla / plugins / modpack?" as
   inputs and *output* a recommended plan. Apex has exactly this mapping (2 GB ≈ 10 players vanilla, 4 GB ≈ 40-mod
   pack, 8–10 GB large modpacks/communities) but leaves it in a guide article instead of the picker.
3. **Recommend explicitly** — one highlighted plan plus use-case badges ("most popular", "good for modpacks") beats a
   grid of specs (Shockbyte's badge approach, minus the RAM-only tiering).
4. **De-risk the choice in the picker itself**: "change plan any time" (Apex allows up/downgrade) removes the fear of
   picking wrong, which is the main hesitation for a first-time buyer.
5. **Signal mod support honestly.** Say precisely what exists — file/SFTP access, a modpack installer, or neither.
   Nxeon already established this honest line on the mods page and must not let the picker overclaim.
6. **Defer software/version/modpack to post-purchase** with a one-click installer (Shockbyte, Aternos).
7. **Free-tier → paid path:** surface the limit *at the moment it bites*, framed as a fact plus an option — during a
   queue wait, at the auto-sleep countdown, at a RAM/storage ceiling, at a player-count cap. Never a generic banner.
   The upgrade must **carry the world/config across**, and that continuity must be promised in the prompt; the fear of
   losing the world is the real blocker, not price.
8. **Keep the panel vocabulary standard** (Console, Files, Backups, Players, Settings, Startup/Network) so users
   arriving from a Pterodactyl-based host are instantly oriented.
9. **Name power actions honestly**, including a Kill that is described as a last resort.

### (i) Pricing transparency principles
1. **Show the renewal/recurring price next to the promotional price, at equal prominence.** Cloudflare (renewal =
   registry list price) and Porkbun (register ≈ renew) both make this the selling point.
2. **Hourly rate + monthly cap together** for anything metered (Hetzner). State that the bill cannot exceed the cap.
3. **State what still bills when a resource is stopped** (Hetzner: a powered-off server still bills for disk and IP).
   Failing to say this is a top source of billing disputes.
4. **Price add-ons as visible deltas** (backups +$X/mo, DDoS +$Y/mo) rather than folding them into a total.
5. **Show a running configuration total** that updates as choices change, plus a final line-item summary before commit.
6. **Tax/VAT/GST:** show it as a named line before the commit action, with the jurisdiction basis, and honour the
   local convention for the customer's region. Never let the charged amount exceed the last figure shown.
7. **Currency:** display in the customer's currency where possible but state the billing currency explicitly if it
   differs, since the card statement will show the billing currency.
8. **No add-ons injected into checkout.** Offer complements before or after, never at the payment step.
9. **Bundle-and-say-so** beats sell-and-upsell for commodity extras (WHOIS privacy, SSL, DNS, forwarding).
10. **Term discounts must show both numbers** — the discounted term rate and the rate after it.

### (j) 12 concrete UX principles Nxeon should adopt

1. **Split every purchase into stage 1 (price-determining fields + payment) and stage 2 (a resumable post-payment
   setup wizard).** WHY: it shortens the path to the money step and moves the intimidating technical decisions to
   after commitment, where the customer is motivated and can be guided. EVIDENCE: Hostinger collects hostname/root
   password/SSH after payment ending in "Finish setup" (hostinger.com/tutorials/how-to-set-up-vps); Shockbyte defers
   server software to a post-purchase installer (shockbyte.com/minecraft).
2. **Ask before payment only what changes the price or is legally required.** WHY: every optional pre-payment field is
   a drop-off point. EVIDENCE: the pre-payment column in (b) — no competitor asks for optional config before the
   commit except Hetzner, whose flow is the longest in the set.
3. **Auto-detect and pre-fill anything inferable; show it as editable rather than asking.** WHY: turns required
   decisions into confirmations. EVIDENCE: Vercel auto-detects framework and build settings and allows
   "Deploy Now" without touching them (vercel.com/docs/getting-started-with-vercel).
4. **Chunk long configuration into 2–3 named stages with explicit advance actions.** WHY: reduces perceived length
   without removing control. EVIDENCE: Vultr's "Configure Software" / "Server Settings" / "Additional Features"
   staging (docs.vultr.com/products/compute/instances/cloud-compute/provisioning).
5. **Model provisioning as named real stages with elapsed time and a p50/p90 expectation; never fake a percentage.**
   WHY: honesty survives the inevitable slow provision; theatre does not. EVIDENCE: Aternos shows queue position and
   ETA; Google states ~10 min / ~1 hr expectations; Cloudflare admits its DNS scan may be incomplete.
6. **Explain any wait's cause, and confirm liveness before consuming scarce capacity.** WHY: an explained wait is
   tolerated; an unexplained one is abandonment. EVIDENCE: Aternos' queue position + ETA + green confirmation step
   before start (support.aternos.org/hc/en-us/articles/360026950812-Queue).
7. **Show registration / renewal / transfer prices side by side at domain-search time, and hourly + monthly cap on
   every compute plan.** WHY: renewal shock and billing surprise are the two biggest trust failures in this industry.
   EVIDENCE: Porkbun's three-column TLD pricing; Cloudflare's at-cost renewal policy
   (developers.cloudflare.com/registrar/); Hetzner's hourly-rate-with-monthly-cap model.
8. **Bundle commodity extras and say they are included; put zero upsells in checkout.** WHY: it differentiates on
   trust, which is Nxeon's competitive lever as an owner-operated host. EVIDENCE: Porkbun bundles WHOIS privacy, SSL,
   forwarding with no checkout upsells; Cloudflare includes WHOIS redaction and DNSSEC.
9. **Turn every incomplete setup into a persistent, resumable task with a visible status — never a modal.** WHY:
   multi-day, externally-dependent setup (DNS, email) cannot live in form state. EVIDENCE: Google Workspace's
   per-domain status column plus standing "Set up Admin Console" prompt.
10. **Make DNS/email verification diagnostic: show queried vs expected, offer registrar-specific steps, and one-click
    "add these records for me" when Nxeon controls the zone.** WHY: turns the hardest step into a button and makes
    failures self-serviceable. EVIDENCE: Google's registrar-specific instructions with a generic fallback; Cloudflare's
    grouped record review during add-site.
11. **Recommend, don't enumerate: take player count and mod intent as picker inputs and output one recommended plan,
    with a visible "change plan any time".** WHY: buyers reason in players, not gigabytes. EVIDENCE: Apex's published
    player-count→RAM mapping exists but only in a guide; Shockbyte badges plans by use case.
12. **Adopt a flat all-products inventory with optional grouping and a default bucket, plus global search across every
    product and attribute.** WHY: Nxeon customers buy across categories, so product-centric nav fragments a single
    site's resources. EVIDENCE: DigitalOcean's optional projects with a default project; Hetzner's hard project
    scoping is the counter-example.

### (k) 8 anti-patterns to avoid

1. **Flat mega-forms.** 15+ visible decisions with no recommended path (Hetzner's 16-step create). Collapsing groups is
   not enough if the *number of groups* stays high.
2. **Fake progress.** Spinners, invented percentages, or stage lists richer than what the backend actually reports.
   Also "Instant Setup" claims that a queue can falsify.
3. **Renewal-price concealment.** A large first-term price with a de-emphasised recurring rate, or long default terms
   whose per-month figure only holds for that term (the pattern to *not* inherit from Nxeon's structural model).
4. **Checkout upsells.** Add-on checkboxes at the payment step, where trust is most fragile.
5. **Undiagnosed verification failure.** "Verification failed" with no indication of what was queried or found —
   directly relevant given Nxeon's own DKIM incident, where a local resolver told the wrong story.
6. **Spec-only plan grids.** RAM-only tiering with no translation to players/workload; and "unlimited slots" claims

   confirmation that only requires clicking OK. Use a separate terminal section, require typing the resource name for
   anything irreversible, and state exactly what is lost.
8. **Hard project/scope walls and product-siloed navigation.** Making the user pick a container before they can do

# The brief said: do NOT assume the two-stage model fits every product. It does not. Here is the
# evidence-based verdict, constrained by HARD RULE 3 (the backend never changes).

Today, order placement creates the Server row AND the PROVISION job in ONE transaction, and the
worker consumes the create-time fields immediately. So moving a create-time field after payment
would mean holding the provision job until setup completes — that is a change to order placement
and provisioning logic, i.e. BACKEND. Therefore:

  A field can move post-payment WITHOUT backend work only if an existing API changes it on a
  LIVE resource. Otherwise it must stay pre-payment (or take a safe default).

This is the test applied below. Competitor practice (Hostinger defers VPS hostname/root/SSH) is
achievable for them because their order pipeline is built for it; ours is not, and we may not change it.

## VERDICT PER PRODUCT

GAME SERVERS — FULL two-stage available today. Biggest win in the portal.
  Pre-pay: game family, tier, term, dedicated IP. That is it.
  Post-pay: serverName (renameServer), subdomain (changeGameSubdomain), variant + EVERY config
  field (saveGameConfig — the phase:"deploy" flag means "needs restart", NOT immutable).
  Effect: 4 steps -> 2. Removes the Minecraft subdomain hard-block, which today stops checkout on
  the highest-volume family for a value that is changeable in one API call afterwards.
  Caveat: required:true schema fields (e.g. Don't Starve TOKEN) must be collected in stage 2 before
  the server can usefully start; surface as a blocking setup task, not a checkout blocker.

SHARED HOSTING — MOSTLY two-stage available.
  Pre-pay: plan, term, extraDiskGB (price, and it has NO post-provision API at all).
  Post-pay: domain/subdomain (createAddonDomain + setPrimaryHostingDomain), app install
  (installApp/installWordPress — already async after ACTIVE, so the wizard step is pure pre-selection).
  Effect: 5 steps -> 2. Also fixes: the Add-ons step is currently 4 read-only "Included" cards.

BUSINESS EMAIL — already short; the real work is ALREADY post-payment and badly supported.
  Pre-pay: domain, plan, term. Post-pay: mailboxes, and the whole DNS verification job.
  Recommendation is not fewer steps but turning post-payment DNS into a persistent, resumable,
  DIAGNOSTIC checklist (show queried vs expected — our own DKIM incident is the argument).

  before registration. Keep them pre-payment; the fix is to ask the contact set ONCE and store it as
  a reusable profile, not to defer it.

input.content:
Nxeon · Customer Portal · Phase 1 deliverable

Portal Redesign Blueprint

A complete audit of what the portal does today, and the design system, information architecture and purchase architecture proposed to replace how it presents it. No code has been changed.

Phase
1 — Audit & blueprint
Status
Ready for review
Date
3 September 2026
Scope
Frontend only
Backend
Unchanged
Evidence
10 code audits
58customer portal routes, sharing one loading and one error boundary
245portal components, ~59,300 lines
214hand-drawn inline SVG icons; no icon library exists
694uses of a secondary text colour that fails contrast on navy
60destructive actions confirmed by the browser's own dialog
0products with any post-payment setup step today
Contents
  1. 01 Executive summary
  2. 02 Current-state diagnosis
  3. 03 Capability inventory
  4. 04 Route inventory
  5. 05 Component & design-system audit
  6. 06 Asset & icon audit
  7. 07 Navigation & IA
  8. 08 Design philosophy
  9. 09 Visual identity
  10. 10 Design tokens
  11. 11 Component system
  12. 12 Motion system
  13. 13 Responsive strategy
  14. 14 Accessibility strategy
  15. 15 VPS architecture
  16. 16 Shared hosting architecture
  17. 17 Game server architecture
  18. 18 Domain architecture
  19. 19 Business email architecture
  20. 20 Purchase & checkout
  21. 21 Post-purchase setup
  22. 22 Dashboard
  23. 23 Account, billing, support
  24. 24 Page hierarchy
  25. 25 User flows
  26. 26 Backend to UI mapping
  27. 27 Must not be removed
  28. 28 Consolidations
  29. 29 Progressive disclosure
  30. 30 Competitor findings
  31. 31 Conversion & psychology
  32. 32 Implementation phases
  33. 33 Implementation order
  34. 34 Risks
  35. 35 Acceptance criteria
01

Executive summary

The Nxeon portal works. Ten read-only audits confirm a large, genuinely capable product: 58 routes, roughly 200 distinct customer capabilities, a real Proxmox-backed VPS platform, a cPanel-class hosting panel, a 47-title game catalogue, a registrar integration, a webmail client and an AI build workspace. Nothing in this blueprint proposes removing any of it.

What the portal lacks is a system. It was assembled feature by feature, and the evidence of that is measurable rather than impressionistic: 21 different spellings of "an inset panel" across about 145 places, eight tab-bar implementations, 24 independent modal implementations alongside 60 native browser confirmations, seven badge implementations, six toggle switches, 18 icon stroke widths, and 385 hand-typed font sizes against a scale that is otherwise ignored. Violet appears 787 times and simultaneously means primary action, selected navigation, informational surface, highlighted text and page background, which is exactly why the interface reads as uniformly purple.

Three conclusions drive everything that follows.

  1. The design system must be built for the portal, not inherited from marketing. Roughly half the existing shared style classes are marketing-only and unused in the portal, while the portal's most repeated patterns have no shared class at all.
  2. Navigation should follow objects, not product names. A game server is a Server row, so clicking one navigates into "Servers" while the sidebar highlight jumps away from "Game Servers". Seven routes have no navigation entry whatsoever.
  3. The purchase funnel is the highest-value work, and the two-stage model fits three of five products, not all of them. Game servers can drop from four steps to two today with no backend change. VPS cannot, and this document says exactly why.

The audits also found live defects. These are correctness problems, not design opinions, and several affect paying customers now. They are listed in section 34 and should be triaged independently of this redesign.

02

Current-state UX diagnosis

Six problems account for most of the "assembled over time" feeling. Each is stated with the evidence that produced it.

D1 · Hierarchy is carried by colour alone

The portal has no display type. Nothing exceeds text-2xl except a single instance, and font-semibold appears 582 times, doing the work of headings, labels, badges, buttons and emphasis at once. With size and weight flattened, the only remaining signal is colour, which is why every page reads as one continuous texture of similar grey-blue blocks.

D2 · Everything is a card, so nothing is

The shared .card class is used 314 times for both real objects and ordinary prose containers, and its own padding is overridden in 63 of those uses. Inside cards, nested surfaces are rebuilt by hand in 21 different recipes. Border and fill no longer mean "this is a distinct object" because they are applied to everything.

D3 · The same idea is implemented many times

Navigation and information architecture

The sidebar is organised by product name — 25 items in 7 groups — while the application is organised by database table. Principle

Navigate by object, not by product name. A customer thinks "my Minecraft server", "my site", "my domain". They never think "a virtual machine with a game plan identifier set". It follows that there should be one detail-page contract per object kind, and the URL should state the kind.

08

The new Nxeon design philosophy

Engineered, not decorated.

Five principles, each stated with the consequence that makes it testable rather than aspirational.

1 · Structure over containers

Hierarchy comes from rules, spacing and alignment, not from wrapping every thought in a bordered rectangle. Consequence: a card must represent an object or an action group. Prose and settings groups get a labelled rule instead. This is the direct fix for the 314 cards and 21 nested panel recipes.

2 · Data is the ornament

The most visually interesting thing on any page should be real information — a metric, a status, an address, a topology. Consequence: no purely decorative graphic inside the app shell. Atmosphere is a single very low-contrast field, never a feature.

3 · One signal colour at a time

Colour means something: brand marks the one primary action here, semantic colour marks state. Consequence: at most one brand-filled control per view region. This is what ends the purple problem, and it is a rule about scarcity rather than about hue.

4 · Progressive power

Every surface answers the beginner in its first screenful and the expert in its second. Consequence: the default view uses outcome language and a recommended configuration; expert controls live on the same page behind a named disclosure, never on a different page and never removed.

5 · Honest machinery

The interface never claims more than the backend knows. Consequence: provisioning states map one-to-one to real backend states. Where the backend only knows "provisioning", the interface says provisioning. Section 21 applies this literally.

09

Proposed visual identity

Navy stays as the foundation, but re-pitched from "purple-blue product" to instrument panel. The reference language is precision instruments, rack elevations, technical drawings and route diagrams. It is explicitly not science-fiction interface, gaming colour, glassmorphism or the gradient-hero look.

Signature elements

These are the details that should make a screenshot identifiably Nxeon without a logo in frame.

The notch

Object surfaces — a server, a domain, a game server, a plan — carry a single small chamfer on one corner. Container surfaces do not. A hardware cue that separates "a thing you own" from "a box holding text" at a glance. Radius elsewhere stays small, never the large pill-like corners used today.

The status filament

A two-pixel edge along the leading side of any resource row or card, carrying state colour. Live and transitional states get a slow travelling highlight; steady states are static. This replaces the dot, pill and coloured-text triple-encoding currently used, and it collapses seven badge implementations into one.

The labelled rule

Section headings sit on a hairline, with a small-caps label and the rule continuing to the edge. This becomes the primary grouping device and removes most card borders. The document you are reading uses it, so the device is visible rather than described.

Data plates

Technical values — addresses, shell commands, identifiers, node names, ports, DNS values, hashes — render on a recessed monospace plate with an integral copy affordance. One treatment everywhere, replacing roughly fifteen different code-value skins and thirteen separate copy-to-clipboard implementations.

The deployment ladder

A vertical, honest provisioning timeline where each rung is a real backend state. This is the signature post-payment moment, specified in section 21.

Topology, not clip art

Regions, networking and infrastructure are drawn as custom vector topology, never flags, stock maps or three-dimensional server illustrations.

VPS UX architecture

58 capabilities, roughly 48 of them on a single detail page built in one render that makes three hypervisor round-trips on every load, including on the five-second refresh cycle during provisioning.

Proposed page hierarchy

  1. Identity band — name, status filament, address on a data plate, region, plan. Always visible.
  2. Primary actions — Start, Restart, Console. Three, no more.
  3. Health — processor, memory, disk, network as live meters with a range selector.
  4. Attention — only when something needs the customer: expiry, failed job, capacity, unpaid balance.
  5. Tabs — Overview, Console, Files, Networking, Storage, Backups, Security, Activity, Settings, and a clearly separated Danger section holding Stop, Reinstall and Destroy.
Why a separate danger sectionToday every destructive action, including Destroy and Reinstall, is confirmed by the browser's own unstyled dialog, and about thirteen of those confirmations say nothing beyond "Delete this?". Destructive controls must not sit at the same visual weight as Restart, and their confirmation must state what happens, what is lost, and whether it can be undone.

Capabilities that must not be lost in the re-layout

The vendored remote console, the terminal over its own websocket service, the file manager over real file transfer, the metrics pipeline with both hypervisor and guest-agent sources, snapshots, the backup tier and schedule, firewall rules and port forwards, the dedicated address purchase, the one-way disk expansion, resize up and down with proration, and the cancellation refund calculation.

Gaps worth surfacing to the owner

Bandwidth is sampled but never shown despite being advertised. Firewall rule reordering exists in code with no interface. Reverse DNS has a column and a helper and no callers. Rescue mode is promised on the marketing page and does not exist. There is no graceful shutdown, only a hard stop. Volumes block reinstall and restore but are never linked from the server page.

Purchase and checkout architecture

The brief asked whether a two-stage model — a short conversion-focused checkout, then an optional post-payment setup — fits every product. It does not, and the reason is specific.

The constraint that decides each case

Order placement today creates the resource and its provisioning job in a single transaction, and the worker consumes the configuration immediately. Deferring a field past payment would mean holding that job until setup completes, which is a change to order placement and provisioning logic — that is backend, and the backend does not change. So the test is narrow and mechanical:

A field can move after payment only if an existing API changes it on a live resource. Otherwise it stays before payment, or takes a safe default.

Stage one asks for game, tier, term and dedicated address. That is all. Everything else moves to setup. This also removes a hard checkout blocker: the connect subdomain is currently mandatory before payment on the highest-volume game family, for a value that a single existing API call changes afterwards.

Five fields the provisioner consumes at creation have no live-change API: the operating system image (only a destructive rebuild), the hostname (the rename action writes a display label only), the SSH key, and two installer add-ons. They cannot move past payment without backend work.

The available win is therefore compression, not deferral: replace four steps and twelve fields with one confirmable recommendation derived from a single question — what are you building? — with everything else defaulted and editable behind one disclosure. The same fields reach the same action; the customer answers one question instead of twelve.

A copy defect to correct either way. The add-ons step tells customers "you can add or remove these later in your VPS dashboard". For the container runtime and the malware scanner this is untrue — both are one-time installer steps with no later control. The wording must change regardless of whether the redesign proceeds.

Cross-cutting checkout fixes

  • Carry the selection through signup. 38 marketing calls to action link to a bare registration page. The registration page already supports a destination parameter and no marketing link sets it, so a visitor who chose a plan and term restarts from nothing.
  • Survive a refresh. Drafts are written continuously but only restored when the checkout was explicitly cancelled. Restore on any return.
  • Close the silent landings. Two status parameters are written by six redirect points and read by none, so a paid-but-unfulfilled order, and every alternative payment return, lands on a page that says nothing.
  • Fix two controls that lie. A cardholder-name field is collected and never used, and a save-card checkbox is rendered checked and disabled, looking like a choice that is not one.
  • Price transparency. Show the term rate and the rate after it at equal prominence, name the tax line with its basis, and state the billing currency where display currency differs. Term discounts must always show both numbers.
  • No upsells at the payment step. Paid add-ons currently hide inside an "advanced options" disclosure on a step headed "additional features" — the revenue is buried under free toggles. Offer them before, or after, never at payment.
21

Post-purchase setup architecture

No product has any post-payment setup step today. The overlay shows read-only progress and then drops the customer onto a full management page.

Stage 1 — Checkout
  • Only what sets the price
  • Only what a registry legally requires
  • Everything else defaulted
  • Ends at payment
Stage 2 — Setup
  • Server-side record, not form state
  • Resumable on any device
  • Skippable, with safe defaults
  • Skipped items become standing tasks

The deployment ladder

This is the signature moment, and its rule is that it never claims more than the system knows. The provisioning worker writes exactly six real step labels; there is no percentage, no estimated time and no status endpoint — progress is polled by refreshing the whole page every five seconds, and when no label exists the interface falls back to text that its own source code describes as cosmetic.

01Allocating your serverreal backend state
02Configuring the networkreal backend state
03Starting your serverreal backend state
04Booting the operating systemreal backend state
05Waiting for network accessreal backend state
06Starting the game servergame orders only

So the ladder shows six rungs and never a percentage. Alongside it: elapsed time and a typical range rather than a countdown; a change of message past the expected window that says so and offers an action instead of spinning silently; connection details revealed the moment they exist, marked not-ready until boot completes; and a page that survives a refresh, a new device and an email link, because provisioning must not depend on a live tab.

Why honesty beats theatre hereA fabricated percentage is only convincing while provisioning is fast. The moment it is slow — the exact moment the customer is most anxious — invented progress becomes visibly wrong and destroys the trust the purchase just built. Named real stages with an explained wait survive that moment.

Setup checklists per product

ProductStage 2 tasks
VPSDeployed, operating system installed, network configured, access ready — then optional application setup, security and backup configuration
GameProvisioned, game installed — then name, connect address, server type and configuration, invite players, mods where genuinely supported
HostingProvisioned, certificate ready — then connect a domain, install an application, create a mailbox
DomainRegistered — then connect a website, configure DNS, enable email, verify ownership
EmailThe six-rung checklist in section 19

One notification gap to close first. Shared hosting sends no email and raises no in-app notification when an account becomes active. A customer who closes the tab is never told their hosting is ready.

22

Dashboard architecture

The home page today is four stat tiles, a server table and two small feeds. It answers "what do I have" and nothing else. It should answer seven questions in this order.

#QuestionSurface
1What needs me?Attention band — expiring domains, failed provisions, unpaid balance, incomplete setup, unverified email. Empty most days, and absent when empty
2What do I have?Estate summary across every kind, including the four currently unreachable ones
3Is it healthy?Status roll-up, using the filament language
4What am I spending?Balance, next charge and its date, monthly run rate
5What happened?Recent activity, filtered to things the customer did or that happened to them
6What should I do next?Standing setup tasks, carried over from stage-two setup
7What can I deploy?Discovery, last — not competing with the estate
Why attention leadsAn infrastructure control centre earns trust by being the place that tells you when something is wrong. Putting discovery first, as the current hero does, optimises the page for a customer who has just arrived rather than the customer who returns every week.
23

Account, billing and support architecture

Billing as a financial control centre

Currently one 944-line page with thirteen stacked sections and no tabs. Proposed: Overview with balance, next charge and run rate; Subscriptions; Invoices as a real tab; Payment methods; Transactions; and Controls for spend caps, auto-recharge and tax details. The recurring-figure calculation is already centralised and shared with the billing worker, which is a genuine strength and must be preserved exactly.

Gaps to close in the interface: there is no promotional code entry for wallet top-ups in production at all, because the field is hidden whenever card payment is configured; there is no way to pay an outstanding invoice from the billing page; and invoice download exists on one route but not on the billing page's own list.

Settings

Four tabs today. Missing entirely and worth adding: email-address change, an active session and device list, timezone, locale and per-account currency. A blunt "sign out everywhere" action currently substitutes for a session list.

Team

Team membership grants no authorization. Ownership checks consult only the individual owner, no data loader consults membership, and the permission field on membership is unused. Four roles are offered, including a billing role, and none of them confers anything. There is also no pending-invite list, no revoke and no ownership transfer.

This is a correctness and expectations problem before it is a design one. The redesign should not present a roles interface that implies capabilities the system does not enforce; either the interface is scoped down to what is true, or enforcement becomes a separate backend project the owner commissions.

Support and notifications

Tickets carry a subject, body and priority only — no category or department, and no attachment on the first message. The chat agent degrades honestly when unavailable, which is the right behaviour and should be kept. The notification model has no kind or severity column, the bell marks everything read on open, and there is no history page.

Around twenty email templates have no production sender. These include server suspended, server terminated, password changed, login alert, low balance and referral reward. Suspension, termination and every security change are classified as critical in the notification policy yet reach the customer only as an in-app bell entry they may never open. This is the highest-priority non-visual finding in the account area.

Activity

Capped at 100 rows with no paging, filtering or export, and several security-relevant actions — password change, session revocation, profile and key edits, gift redemption — write no audit row at all. Impersonated entries expose a raw internal identifier with no explanation.

24

Recommended page hierarchy

Every page in the portal takes the same skeleton. Where a page needs to differ it should be deliberately special, not accidentally inconsistent.

APP SHELL ├── Sidebar — product architecture, adapts to the estate ├── Top bar — search, currency, notifications, account menu ├── Page header — context, title, status, one primary action ├── Attention — only when something needs the customer ├── Content — one content width, one section rule, one grid └── Support layer — persistent, never competing with the page
Route familyShape
HomeAttention → estate → health → spend → activity → tasks → discover
Resource listHeader with primary action → filters → object rows with filaments → empty state with an action
Resource detailIdentity → primary actions → health → attention → tabs → danger section
PurchaseStage bar → one decision per step → persistent price summary → payment
SetupLadder or checklist → per-task detail → skip → completion
Settings-likeLeft navigation or tabs → grouped by labelled rule → one form structure
EditorialActivity, what's new, tools: single column at reading width

Every page must have clear context, a title, one clear primary action, visible status, one content width, consistent spacing and typography, consistent components and actions, and defined responsive behaviour.

25

Recommended user flows

FlowShapeFirst value
Buy a VPSDiscover → plan and term → confirm recommendation → pay → ladder → readyFirst successful login
Buy a game serverGame → tier and term → pay → ladder → setup → inviteFirst player connects
Buy hostingPlan and term → pay → ladder → connect a domain → installFirst site online
Buy a domainSearch → availability with registration, renewal and transfer prices → contacts once → pay → next actionDomain connected
Set up emailDomain and plan → pay → six-rung diagnostic checklistFirst message sent and received
Free tier to paidLimit is reached → the fact and the option, stated where it bites → upgrade carries the world acrossContinuity, promised explicitly
Something is wrongAttention on home → the affected object → what happened, why, how to fix → retry or contact supportResolution without a ticket
Why the free-to-paid prompt is placed at the limitThe blocker for a free-tier player is not price, it is the fear of losing their world. The prompt therefore has to appear at the moment a limit actually bites and must promise continuity in the prompt itself, not in a generic upgrade banner.
26

Backend capability to new UI mapping

The redesign consumes the same APIs. This table states where each backend area surfaces in the new structure, so nothing is stranded.

Backend areaNew home

Snapshots, backups, schedulesResource detail: Backups tab; restore confirmations state what is lost

Tickets, chat agent, knowledge baseAccount: Support, plus the persistent support layer

27

Features that must not be removed

These are at highest risk because they are easy to miss in a re-layout: they sit behind a tab, a disclosure or a route with no navigation entry.

  • The remote console, the terminal service and the file transfer implementation — three separate integrations that must be carried across unchanged.
  • The 37-action database studio inside hosting.
  • The full webmail client: composer with drafts that survive navigation, signatures, aliases, forwarding, auto-reply, and the rule-status check that reports when the mail server is not actually running a saved rule.
  • The deliverability panel that reports pass, warning, fail and unknown without ever rounding unknown up to pass.
  • The DNS quick-setup presets and the one-click record creation where Nxeon controls the zone.
  • Resize up and down with proration, the cancellation refund calculation, spend caps, auto-recharge and the tax context.
  • The idempotent fulfilment path and its promotional reserve, confirm and release protocol — a correctness mechanism, not a feature.
  • The free-tier management panel in full: modes, presets, permissions, inventory editor and the public directory.
  • The migration remediation and re-check flow, whose verdict only ever improves.
  • The AI build workspace's plan-then-approve mode and its command limits.
  • The chat agent's honest degradation, and the operator-visible record of it.
28

Features that should be consolidated

ConsolidateIntoWhy
Servers, Game Servers, Free Minecraft, NxCloud, Volumes, Sites as separate list surfacesOne Resources inventory with kind filtersEnds the label-versus-URL contradiction and rehomes four orphans
The two parallel control panelsOne panel with per-product capability gatingWebsites, databases, cron, apps and files are implemented twice today
Referrals and affiliateOne programme pageSame code, same reward, presented twice; one has no navigation entry
The builder and its guides hubOne Build surface with a Guides tabTwo adjacent entries whose labels are swapped relative to their URLs
Invoices as a separate routeA Billing tabThe navigation already claims this happened; it has not
FeedbackSupportReachable today only from one inline link and a floating widget

Five tab mechanisms, 24 modals, 60 browser confirms, 6 toggles, 13 copy buttonsOne primitive eachSection 11
29

What should use progressive disclosure

The rule: simple by default, powerful when expanded, never removed and never on another page.

SurfaceDefault viewBehind a named disclosure
VPS purchasePlan, term, and one recommendationImage, hostname, key, add-ons, storage, backup tier
Game purchaseGame, tier, termEverything else, moved to setup entirely
Server detailIdentity, three actions, healthNetworking, security, storage, advanced, danger
Domain detailIdentity, setup progress, core actionsNameservers, privacy, lock, transfer out, bulk DNS tools
EmailThe checklist and mailboxesRaw records, deliverability internals, connection settings
BillingBalance, next charge, run rateSpend caps, auto-recharge, tax details, ledger
MetricsFour meters and a rangePer-metric detail, longer ranges, raw values
Why "never on another page"Moving an advanced control to a separate route is how the portal acquired seven orphans. Disclosure keeps the expert's control one click away and in context, while the beginner never has to see it.
30

Competitor and industry findings

Fourteen products were studied for flow structure and principle only. No visual design, branding, layout or copy was captured, and nothing here is a template to copy.

The decisive finding

Across every competitor selling to non-experts, the only fields asked before payment are those that determine the price and those a third party legally requires. The one exception in the set is also the longest and most criticised flow. Two-stage checkout is already standard: one large multi-product host collects hostname, root password and key after payment, ending in an explicit "finish setup"; two major game hosts defer game software and modpack entirely to a post-purchase installer; and a major workspace provider defers its whole DNS and mailbox setup.

Provisioning honesty

The strongest example in the category is a free game host that shows queue position and an estimate, confirms the player is still present before consuming capacity, and shows a visible countdown before sleeping a server. It exposes a scarcity constraint rather than concealing it, and players tolerate it — which is the whole argument for named real stages over invented percentages.

Other principles worth adopting

  • Show registration, renewal and transfer prices together at domain-search time. This is the single highest-trust intervention in that category.
  • State what still bills when a resource is stopped. Failing to say this is a leading source of billing disputes.
  • Bundle commodity extras and say they are included, rather than selling them at checkout.
  • Make verification diagnostic, with registrar-specific guidance and a one-click "add these records for me" wherever Nxeon controls the zone.
  • For game plans, take player count and mod intent as inputs and output one recommendation — buyers reason in players, not gigabytes — with a visible "change plan any time" to de-risk the choice.
  • Prefer a flat inventory with optional grouping over hard project scoping, which degrades cross-product search for customers who buy across categories.

The anti-pattern closest to home. Long default terms whose attractive monthly figure only holds for that term. Nxeon's structural model makes this easy to inherit; section 20 requires both numbers at equal prominence precisely to avoid it.

31

Buyer psychology and conversion

  1. Every optional pre-payment field is a place to leave. This is the entire thesis of section 20, and the reason game servers are the first funnel to rebuild.
  2. Turn decisions into confirmations. A recommendation the customer approves converts better than a blank form, and it lets a beginner buy infrastructure without becoming an infrastructure expert.
  3. Never lose work. A refresh currently discards a whole wizard. Restoring drafts on any return is a conversion fix, not a convenience.
  4. Carry intent across the signup boundary. Thirty-eight marketing links currently discard the plan the visitor just chose.
  5. Answer the seven checkout questions without hunting: what am I buying, why this one, what does it cost, what do I pay today, what later, where will it run, and what happens after I pay.
  6. Make the recommended badge mean something. The "popular" marker is currently assigned by position in the list rather than by any signal.
  7. Design the post-payment moment. The customer has just paid and is asking whether it worked. The ladder answers that in the first second, and first value — the address, the credentials, the connect string — appears the moment it exists.
  8. Trust is the differentiator available to an owner-operated host. Transparent renewal pricing, no checkout upsells, honest capability claims and diagnostic errors are cheaper to build than they are to imitate.
32

Implementation phases

All implementation happens in an isolated sandbox with no real backend connectivity — no live payment provider, no registrar, no customer data — and nothing is promoted until reviewed. This blueprint authorises none of it; phase 2 begins only on the owner's approval.

PhaseWorkExit condition
2Design system: tokens, type scale, icon set, the four surface archetypes, and a style-guide routeEvery primitive rendered in both themes at every state
3App shell: sidebar, top bar, page header, content contract, command paletteOne page shape, one content width, one tab mechanism
4Navigation and IA, including rehoming all seven orphansNo route without a navigational home
5Purchase and deployment: stage one, the ladder, stage two setupGame at two steps; hosting at two; VPS compressed to two
6DashboardAnswers all seven questions in order
7–11Product surfaces: VPS, game, hosting, domains, emailEvery capability in section 3 reachable
12Billing, account, team, support, activityInvoices a real tab; no capability claimed that is not enforced
13Remaining surfaces: volumes, NxCloud, sites, build, migration, toolsConsistent with the system
14Responsive and mobileTables become cards; no page scrolls sideways
15AccessibilitySection 14 targets met and verified
