Here's the handoff prompt. Copy this whole block into a fresh session:

```
NXEON DESIGN SYSTEM — POLISH PASS
Phase 2 continuation. Do not start Phase 3.

==================================================
CONTEXT — READ THIS FIRST
==================================================

Phase 2 (the Nxeon design system) was already built by a prior session at
/opt/nxeon-designsystem. It is a complete, isolated Next.js app: design tokens,
a 60-icon family, four surface archetypes (object/container/plate/rule), a
full component library, a canvas-based rotating globe, five per-product
deployment loaders, and a showcase route at /design that documents all of it.

Before touching anything, read these three files in full:
  1. /opt/nxeon-designsystem/README.md
  2. /root/.claude/projects/-root/memory/nxeon-design-system-phase2.md
  3. /root/.claude/projects/-root/memory/nxeon-brand-gradient.md
Also check the memory index at /root/.claude/projects/-root/memory/MEMORY.md
for any other nxeon-* entries relevant to this project (there is one about a
past pkill incident — read it, it matters for the safety rules below).

Do NOT trust memory files over the actual code. If something in memory
disagrees with what you find in the repo, the repo is the truth — the
memory may be stale or describe something that was later changed.

This is NOT a rebuild. The system, the tokens, the four surface archetypes,
the icon set, the globe, the deploy loaders and the component library are
all APPROVED. Your job is to tighten what exists, not redesign it.

==================================================
CRITICAL: ISOLATION AND PRODUCTION SAFETY
==================================================

/opt/nxeon-designsystem is a from-scratch, isolated project — no .env file,
no database client, no payment/registrar/mail/hypervisor SDK, no fetch() to
anything, zero runtime dependencies beyond next/react/react-dom. Keep it
that way. Do not add a backend call, an environment variable, or any
dependency that talks to a real service.

DO NOT touch /opt/nxeon, /opt/nxeon-staging, or /opt/nxeon-sandbox. Those are
the real production, staging, and an older sandbox tree. Read-only if you
need to reference something (e.g. a token you're unsure about), never write.

The sandbox runs as a manually started process on port 3010 (not systemd,
not in nginx's main config). It is reverse-proxied for review at:
  https://flow.k9x4rq7wpz2ah6t.nxeon.cloud/ds/design
via a `location /ds/` block added to the EXISTING nxeon-sandbox nginx vhost,
protected by basic auth. Credentials: user "nxeon", password in
/root/.ds-review-password (read it, don't ask the owner to repeat it).
Do not touch nginx config or that vhost. If the app on :3010 isn't running,
restart it yourself with `cd /opt/nxeon-designsystem && npx next start -p 3010`
run detached (setsid nohup ... &).

NEVER kill processes by a generic command-line pattern (no `pkill -f "next"`,
no `pkill -f "next start"`, no `killall node`). Every Node service on this
host — prod, staging, this sandbox — shares similar command lines, and a
pattern match has taken production down before. To stop only this sandbox,
find its PID by the port it's bound to and kill that PID specifically:
  PID=$(ss -ltnpH 'sport = :3010' | grep -oP 'pid=\K[0-9]+' | head -1)
  [ -n "$PID" ] && kill "$PID"
Verify production is unaffected after any restart:
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:3000/
  (expect 200 — that's the real production app, do not disturb it)

==================================================
WHAT "POLISH" MEANS HERE
==================================================

Go through the whole system with a fine comb. Concretely:

1. CONSISTENCY AUDIT
   - Every `.nx-object` usage: confirm the notch (chamfer) renders correctly
     with a real border along the diagonal, not a clipped-off edge. Check
     every place the pattern is used (checkout plan cards, game cards,
     inventory rows, region cards) at multiple widths — a rushed addition
     may have gotten the clip-path direction or size wrong somewhere.
   - Glow discipline: the rule is "at most one glow per surface" (nx-glow-soft
     / nx-glow-card / nx-glow-hero / nx-lift). Audit every page in app/design/
     and flag/fix any surface that stacks two, or where a glow was added
     without a clear reason.
   - Colour discipline: grep the whole components/ and app/ tree for any raw
     hex, rgb(), or arbitrary Tailwind colour value that isn't a token
     reference. There should be none in components; a couple in globals.css
     are expected (that's where tokens are defined) — everywhere else is a
     violation to fix.
   - Typography discipline: grep for arbitrary text-[...] sizes outside the
     defined scale (display/h1-h4/body/body-sm/caption/label/code/metric).
     Flag anything that snuck in.
   - KNOWN INCONSISTENCY TO FIX: the two-stage checkout pattern
     (app/design/patterns.tsx, Checkout function) still uses the flat SVG
     RegionMap component for its region step, while the dedicated "Region
     selector" showcase page (app/design/showpieces.tsx, Regions function)
     uses the much better Globe component. Decide whether checkout should
     use a compact version of the Globe instead for consistency, or whether
     RegionMap is deliberately the "inline/compact" variant and Globe is
     the "hero" variant — either is defensible, but make it a considered
     decision and document which, not an oversight.

2. ACCESSIBILITY RE-VERIFICATION
   A lot of visual work (glows, gradients, neon) landed fast late in the
   build and was not re-checked against the accessibility bar the tokens
   were originally built to hit. Re-verify:
   - Contrast of white text sitting on the brand gradient (e.g. the
     "Popular"/"Recommended" badges, the deploy button label) at actual
     rendered sizes — gradients can dip below AA at some points along the
     ramp even if the endpoints are fine.
   - That focus rings are still visibly distinguishable on surfaces that
     now carry a glow shadow (the glow and the focus ring can visually
     compete or the ring can get lost).
   - That every new animation added late (globe rotation, deploy loader
     loops, the sweep/trace effects) is actually caught by the global
     `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` rule in globals.css — trace it
     through, don't assume.
   - Re-run the label/association check on any new form-like controls
     added in the later patches (game picker, region cards) — confirm
     they're real buttons with aria-pressed, not divs with onClick.

3. PERFORMANCE
   - The globe (components/system/Globe.tsx) runs a requestAnimationFrame
     loop with ~20k points unconditionally, even when scrolled off-screen
     or on an inactive tab. Add an IntersectionObserver (or similar) to
     pause the rAF loop when the canvas isn't visible, and confirm
     document.visibilityState is respected too.
   - Check for any other unconditional animation loops with the same issue.
   - Run `npx next build` and confirm a clean production build: zero
     TypeScript errors, no new warnings introduced.

4. RESPONSIVE RE-CHECK
   Mobile (bottom nav, table-to-cards, bottom-sheet modals, sticky action
   bars, pinned checkout price) was the last thing built. Do a full sweep
   at 390px, 768px, and 1440px across every entry in the showcase sidebar
   and confirm: no horizontal overflow anywhere, the bottom nav's "More"
   drawer opens and traps focus correctly, and nothing added in the polish
   pass itself (e.g. a new glow or a wider hero) reintroduces overflow.

5. DENSITY
   Multiple pages (dashboard-style overview cards, some Container blocks)
   still read as airy/documentation-style rather than an infrastructure
   control surface. Tighten spacing and information density where it's
   clearly excessive — but don't fight the type scale or section-rule
   rhythm to do it; those are settled.

==================================================
HOW TO VERIFY YOUR WORK
==================================================

Use Playwright via the vendored chromium (same approach the prior session
used — check /opt/nxeon/node_modules/playwright-core and
/root/.cache/ms-playwright/ for the binary path) to screenshot every
sidebar entry at desktop (1440px), tablet (768px), and mobile (390px), and
actually look at the screenshots before claiming something is fixed.

After any code change: `npx next build` must succeed. Restart the dev
server on :3010 (port-specific kill only, see safety rules) and re-verify
the public review URL still returns 200 with auth
(`curl -u nxeon:$(cat /root/.ds-review-password) ...`) and 401 without it.

==================================================
WHAT NOT TO DO
==================================================

- Do not touch the magenta placeholder value (--color-brand-c in
  app/globals.css). It is intentionally a placeholder pending the owner's
  exact brand hex — read nxeon-brand-gradient.md before going anywhere
  near it. Do not guess a "better" value.
- Do not add new component categories or new pages to the showcase beyond
  what's needed to demonstrate a fix. This is a polish pass, not Phase 3.
- Do not migrate anything into the real /opt/nxeon portal. That is a later
  phase and requires separate owner approval.
- Do not add a git repo, CI config, or any tooling not already present
  unless it's directly needed to do the verification above.

==================================================
WHEN DONE
==================================================

Report: what you found in the consistency audit (with counts, like the
prior session's own findings — "N surfaces had a double glow", "N raw hex
values found"), what you fixed, the before/after on any a11y or perf issue,
and confirm the production build is clean and the review URL is live.
Do not start Phase 3.
```

A few notes on why it's shaped this way:

- It front-loads the memory files rather than re-explaining everything, since Fable will have MEMORY.md auto-injected and can read the full files from there — that saves you re-pasting context and keeps this prompt shorter.
- I flagged the checkout using the flat `RegionMap` instead of the `Globe` as a specific known inconsistency, since it's real and I noticed it while building but never resolved it.
- I verified before writing this: the sandbox is up on port 3010, the public review URL correctly returns 401 without auth, and the credential file exists at `/root/.ds-review-password` — the prompt points to the file rather than embedding the password in plain text.
- The pkill safety rule is repeated explicitly rather than just cited, since a mid-session slip on that cost real production downtime earlier in this project.

That confirms it plainly: **this is not a finished product, and it was never meant to be one at this stage.** It's the foundation layer only. Here's the honest breakdown.

**What actually exists.** One route. Everything lives inside a single showcase page that switches between in-memory views — there is no `app/dashboard`, no per-product pages, no real routing at all. The navigation you see is organized as documentation categories, Foundations, Components, Patterns, not as the actual product information architecture the blueprint proposed.

**What the "Patterns" section really is.** Nine demonstrations, each showing the system applied to one representative case: one inventory list, one generic resource detail page, one checkout flow, one deployment ladder, one region selector, one game catalogue. These prove the components work under real-ish conditions. They are not the actual flows for your five products. The checkout demo styles itself like a game-server purchase, but shared hosting, domains, VPS, and email each need their own checkout with different fields, and only the shape was validated, not each one built.

**What has zero coverage right now**, measured against the roughly two hundred capabilities the Phase 1 audit catalogued:

- The real VPS control panel — console, files, snapshots, backups, networking, firewall, resize. One generic detail page stands in for all of it.
- Shared hosting entirely — the 48-capability panel, the database studio, cron, apps, none of it built.
- Domains — no DNS table, no registration flow, no WHOIS or transfer screens.
- Business email — the six-step verification checklist was designed in the blueprint but never built as a component.
- Billing, account settings, team, support, activity, referrals — nothing.
- Free Minecraft, migration, volumes, NxCloud, sites, the AI builder — nothing.
- The actual customer dashboard the blueprint specified — attention band, estate summary, spend — doesn't exist; only a documentation-style overview page does.

**On assets specifically**, you're right to flag it. The icon set is real and complete. Everything else in the Phase 1 asset audit is still open: there's no real vector master for your logo, the game catalogue uses procedurally generated color gradients standing in for key art, not the actual Steam-sourced artwork sitting in your production repo, and none of the KEEP or REPLACE decisions from that audit have been executed.

**What is correctly out of scope**, not missing: backend integration. I just confirmed there is no `fetch`, no database client, no Stripe, nothing live anywhere in the tree. That's by design for this phase and stays that way until you approve an integration phase — it's not a gap, it's a boundary.

So in terms of the blueprint's own seventeen-phase plan, this is Phase 2 of 16 remaining. Phase 3 is the real app shell and navigation wired to actual routes. Then the purchase funnel for all five products for real. Then each product surface individually. Then account and billing. That's the order the blueprint itself set, because the purchase funnel is where the money is and shouldn't wait behind product pages.

NXEON PORTAL REDESIGN — PHASE 3
APPLICATION SHELL + NAVIGATION + INFORMATION ARCHITECTURE

PHASE 1 — AUDIT / BLUEPRINT
PHASE 2 — DESIGN SYSTEM
PHASE 2 POLISH — COMPLETE

We are now beginning PHASE 3.

Use the approved Phase 1 blueprint and the completed Phase 2 design system as the source of truth.

==================================================
CRITICAL PRODUCTION SAFETY
==================================================

DO NOT MODIFY THE CURRENT RUNNING/PRODUCTION NXEON APPLICATION.

The existing Nxeon application is READ-ONLY.

Work ONLY inside the isolated redesign sandbox.

The sandbox must have:

- No production backend connection
- No production database
- No production credentials
- No production API calls
- No real provisioning
- No real billing
- No real domain operations
- No real customer actions

Use mocked/local data where necessary.

If there is any possibility that an operation could affect production:

STOP.

==================================================
PHASE 3 OBJECTIVE
==================================================

Turn the Phase 2 design system into the actual foundation of the redesigned Nxeon portal.

This phase is specifically about:

1. Application shell
2. Global navigation
3. Information architecture
4. Global search / command experience
5. Workspace/account context
6. Responsive navigation
7. Global page layout patterns

DO NOT redesign individual product pages yet.

==================================================
IMPORTANT: DO NOT JUST RESTYLE THE OLD SHELL
==================================================

The existing Nxeon sidebar should NOT simply receive new colors, typography and spacing.

Rebuild the shell using the approved Phase 1 IA.

The objective is to make navigation dramatically easier to understand.

The user should immediately understand:

- Where they are
- What they own
- What they can manage
- What requires attention
- How to create/deploy something
- Where billing/account functions live
- Where support is available

Reduce unnecessary cognitive load.

==================================================
GLOBAL NAVIGATION
==================================================

Implement the approved navigation architecture from Phase 1.

Use clear product groupings and hierarchy.

Avoid:

- Excessive navigation items
- Random grouping
- Duplicate destinations
- Deep nesting
- Unclear terminology
- Decorative navigation sections

Navigation labels should be concise and user-oriented.

Differentiate between:

PRODUCT AREAS

and

ACCOUNT / OPERATIONS / SUPPORT

Do not make users mentally determine which items are products versus account functions.

==================================================
SIDEBAR
==================================================

Create the new Nxeon sidebar using Phase 2 components.

It should support:

- Expanded state
- Collapsed state
- Active state
- Hover state
- Keyboard focus
- Group expansion
- Responsive/mobile behavior

The active destination must be immediately obvious.

Do not rely only on a subtle background color.

The sidebar should feel like part of the Nxeon product, not a generic dashboard template.

Use the Phase 2 icon system exclusively.

Do not introduce another icon library.

==================================================
RESOURCE / PRODUCT CONTEXT
==================================================

Nxeon manages many different resource types:

- VPS
- Game Servers
- Shared Hosting
- Domains
- Email
- Volumes
- etc.

Create the shell patterns necessary to support contextual navigation.

For example, when a user enters a specific server, the interface should clearly establish:

Nxeon
→ Compute
→ VPS
→ Server Name

Similarly for:

Domain
Game Server
Website
Mailbox
etc.

Do not yet redesign those individual resource pages.

Build only the navigation/context foundation they will use later.

==================================================
TOP BAR
==================================================

Implement the redesigned global top bar.

It should provide the appropriate combination of:

- Global search
- Command launcher
- Notifications
- Workspace/account selector
- User/account controls

Do not overcrowd it.

The top bar should establish a consistent global location for global actions.

==================================================
GLOBAL SEARCH / COMMAND EXPERIENCE
==================================================

Build the foundation for Nxeon's global search/command interface.

It should eventually allow users to find things such as:

- Servers
- Domains
- Websites
- Game servers
- Mailboxes
- Billing
- Settings
- Support
- Actions

It should support a keyboard shortcut.

Create realistic mocked results.

The experience should feel significantly more useful than a simple text search.

Think:

"Where is the thing I need?"

rather than:

"Search this page."

Include:

- Recent items
- Search results
- Categories
- Actions
- Keyboard navigation
- Empty state
- No-results state

==================================================
PAGE HEADER SYSTEM
==================================================

Implement the global page-header pattern created in Phase 2.

It should support:

- Breadcrumb/context
- Page title
- Description
- Status
- Primary action
- Secondary actions
- Overflow actions

The hierarchy must be consistent throughout the portal.

Do not allow every page to invent its own header structure.

==================================================
GLOBAL CONTENT LAYOUT
==================================================

Establish the standard Nxeon content architecture.

Define:

- Page width
- Page gutters
- Header spacing
- Section spacing
- Content density
- Responsive behavior
- Action placement

Avoid making every page a collection of cards.

The shell should support:

- Tables
- Lists
- Forms
- Dashboards
- Resource pages
- Wizards
- Technical interfaces
- Empty states

without requiring a completely different layout system.

==================================================
GLOBAL STATES
==================================================

Establish shell-level handling for:

- Loading
- Empty
- Error
- Offline
- Permission denied
- Not found

Create the global patterns now so later product pages can consume them.

==================================================
NOTIFICATIONS
==================================================

Build the global notification foundation.

Notifications should be structured around:

- Important infrastructure events
- Billing events
- Security events
- System notices
- Product updates

Do not create a noisy notification center.

Use priority and grouping.

==================================================
ACCOUNT / WORKSPACE CONTEXT
==================================================

Create the reusable account/workspace selector pattern if supported by the blueprint.

The user should always understand which account/workspace they are operating within.

Do not expose unnecessary technical information.

==================================================
RESPONSIVE BEHAVIOR
==================================================

Design the shell explicitly for:

- Large desktop
- Desktop
- Laptop
- Tablet
- Mobile

On mobile:

- Sidebar should become an appropriate navigation drawer/sheet
- Top bar should simplify
- Global search should remain accessible
- Important actions should remain reachable
- Content should not simply be horizontally compressed

Test the actual interaction rather than only resizing the browser.

==================================================
ACCESSIBILITY
==================================================

The shell must support:

- Keyboard navigation
- Visible focus
- Logical tab order
- Semantic navigation
- Accessible labels
- Screen-reader-friendly states
- Reduced motion

Navigation cannot depend solely on color or iconography.

==================================================
PRODUCT PAGE MIGRATION RULE
==================================================

DO NOT redesign the actual product pages in this phase.

That means:

DO NOT redesign:

- VPS Overview
- VPS Control Panel
- VPS Metrics
- VPS Console
- VPS Files
- Game Server
- Shared Hosting
- Domain Management
- Business Email
- Billing
- Support
- Settings
- etc.

The purpose of this phase is to create the shell that those pages will eventually live inside.

If necessary, create simple placeholder/demo routes using mocked content to demonstrate how future pages will sit inside the shell.

==================================================
FUNCTIONALITY
==================================================

Preserve all existing routes and capabilities in the sandbox.

Do not delete routes simply because they haven't been redesigned yet.

If navigation labels or grouping change, ensure every existing destination remains reachable.

Create a clear route/capability mapping if necessary.

Do not invent functionality.

Do not connect anything to production.

==================================================
QUALITY BAR
==================================================

The finished shell should feel like a completely new Nxeon application.

It should NOT feel like:

"the old sidebar with a new theme."

It should feel like:

"a new product architecture built around the Nxeon Design System."

Pay particular attention to:

- Navigation hierarchy
- Spatial rhythm
- Active states
- Information density
- Typography
- Context
- Search
- Responsive behavior
- Micro-interactions

The result should feel premium, technically sophisticated and extremely intentional.

==================================================
PHASE 3 EXIT CONDITION
==================================================

Phase 3 is complete when:

1. New Nxeon application shell is implemented.
2. New sidebar is implemented.
3. New top bar is implemented.
4. New global search/command experience is implemented.
5. Navigation/IA is implemented according to Phase 1.
6. Page-header architecture is implemented.
7. Global content layout is implemented.
8. Account/workspace context is implemented where applicable.
9. Notification foundation is implemented.
10. Responsive shell behavior works.
11. Accessibility foundations work.
12. All existing destinations remain reachable in the sandbox.
13. No production systems were touched.
14. No major product pages were redesigned.

==================================================
STOP CONDITION
==================================================

DO NOT automatically continue to Phase 4.

When complete:

- Summarize what was implemented.
- List important files/components changed.
- Explain any IA decisions or deviations.
- Explain any technical issues discovered.
- Confirm production was untouched.
- Confirm no product surfaces were migrated.

Then state:

"PHASE 3 COMPLETE — NXEON APPLICATION SHELL READY FOR REVIEW"

STOP AND WAIT.

=== IA PROPOSAL DRAFT ===
# IA PROPOSAL DRAFT (blueprint section 7) — grounded in audit-01

## The core diagnosis to fix
The sidebar is organised by PRODUCT NAME (25 items, 7 groups) while the app is organised by
BACKEND TABLE. Game servers are `Server` rows, so a game server's detail page is
/dashboard/servers/{id}: label, URL and nav highlight disagree on every click. NxCloud is a
fourth Server-backed product hidden from the Servers list with no nav entry. Nothing in the
sidebar is contextual to what the customer owns: one VPS or a full estate, both see 21 rows.

## Principle
Navigate by OBJECT, not by product-name. A customer thinks "my Minecraft server", "my site",
"my domain", "my mailbox". They never think "a Proxmox VM with gamePlanId set".
Corollary: one detail-page contract per object KIND, and the URL says what the object is.

## Proposed structure (6 top-level, plus contextual object routes)

HOME                     the estate: what I have, what needs me, what I'm spending
DEPLOY                   one hub, ALL purchasable things (today it covers 4 of ~11)
RESOURCES                one unified inventory of everything I own, filterable by kind
  - the list is ONE surface with kind filters (VPS - Game - Hosting - Site - Volume -
    NxCloud - Free Minecraft), not five sidebar rows over two backends
  - object routes become /dashboard/r/{kind}/{id} so the URL states the kind and the nav
    highlight is always right. Existing /dashboard/servers/{id} keeps working as a redirect
    (frontend-only change; no backend contract moves)
DOMAINS & MAIL           domains, DNS, SSL, mailboxes, inbox - the "identity" cluster
  - SSL moves here from its own row: it is an attribute of a domain, not a product
BUILD                    the AI builder (today "Matrix" at /dashboard/build) + the guides hub
  (today mislabelled "Build with AI" at /dashboard/claude-code) merged into ONE surface with
  a Guides tab. Two adjacent AI rows whose labels are swapped vs their URLs is indefensible.
ACCOUNT                  billing (invoices as a real tab), team, support, activity, referrals,
  partner, settings, what's new

Tools (16 utilities) demote from a sidebar row to a command-palette surface + a footer link;
they are duplicated verbatim at /tools/* on marketing and do not earn permanent nav weight.
Server Directory leaves the sidebar: it ejects the customer into the marketing layout.

## Rules the new IA must enforce
1. Every route has a nav home. Kills the seven orphans: nxcloud, projects, invoices,
   affiliate, feedback, free-minecraft, order. Projects becomes a grouping FILTER on Resources
   rather than a hidden page; invoices becomes a Billing tab; order dies; free-minecraft
   becomes a kind filter with the old URL kept as a redirect for marketing deep links.
2. One tab mechanism, URL-addressable, Back-safe. Today there are five, and the two most-used
   (ServerTabs, HostingTabs) use replaceState so Back exits the page and ?tab= only works on
   first render. New rule: tabs are real routes or pushState, always deep-linkable.
3. One page-shell contract. Today: 34 pages PortalHero, 4 PageHeader, 2 neither, 1 bare h1,
   1 aria-hidden void. One PageHeader primitive, one content width, one section rule.
4. The sidebar adapts to the estate. Kinds the customer owns are pinned; kinds they don't own
   collapse into "Explore" under Deploy. A one-VPS customer should not carry 21 rows.
5. The command palette becomes a real command palette: actions (deploy, add funds, restart,
   open ticket) plus the 8 entity types currently unindexed (volumes, SSL, invoices, projects,
   sites, nxcloud, migrations, free-MC).

# IA PROPOSAL DRAFT (blueprint section 7) — grounded in audit-01

## The core diagnosis to fix
The sidebar is organised by PRODUCT NAME (25 items, 7 groups) while the app is organised by
BACKEND TABLE. Game servers are `Server` rows, so a game server's detail page is
/dashboard/servers/{id}: label, URL and nav highlight disagree on every click. NxCloud is a
fourth Server-backed product hidden from the Servers list with no nav entry. Nothing in the
sidebar is contextual to what the customer owns: one VPS or a full estate, both see 21 rows.

## Principle
Navigate by OBJECT, not by product-name. A customer thinks "my Minecraft server", "my site",
"my domain", "my mailbox". They never think "a Proxmox VM with gamePlanId set".
Corollary: one detail-page contract per object KIND, and the URL says what the object is.

## Proposed structure (6 top-level, plus contextual object routes)

HOME                     the estate: what I have, what needs me, what I'm spending
DEPLOY                   one hub, ALL purchasable things (today it covers 4 of ~11)
RESOURCES                one unified inventory of everything I own, filterable by kind
  - the list is ONE surface with kind filters (VPS - Game - Hosting - Site - Volume -
    NxCloud - Free Minecraft), not five sidebar rows over two backends
  - object routes become /dashboard/r/{kind}/{id} so the URL states the kind and the nav
    highlight is always right. Existing /dashboard/servers/{id} keeps working as a redirect
    (frontend-only change; no backend contract moves)
DOMAINS & MAIL           domains, DNS, SSL, mailboxes, inbox - the "identity" cluster
  - SSL moves here from its own row: it is an attribute of a domain, not a product
BUILD                    the AI builder (today "Matrix" at /dashboard/build) + the guides hub
  (today mislabelled "Build with AI" at /dashboard/claude-code) merged into ONE surface with
  a Guides tab. Two adjacent AI rows whose labels are swapped vs their URLs is indefensible.
ACCOUNT                  billing (invoices as a real tab), team, support, activity, referrals,
  partner, settings, what's new

Tools (16 utilities) demote from a sidebar row to a command-palette surface + a footer link;
they are duplicated verbatim at /tools/* on marketing and do not earn permanent nav weight.
Server Directory leaves the sidebar: it ejects the customer into the marketing layout.

## Rules the new IA must enforce
1. Every route has a nav home. Kills the seven orphans: nxcloud, projects, invoices,
   affiliate, feedback, free-minecraft, order. Projects becomes a grouping FILTER on Resources
   rather than a hidden page; invoices becomes a Billing tab; order dies; free-minecraft
   becomes a kind filter with the old URL kept as a redirect for marketing deep links.
2. One tab mechanism, URL-addressable, Back-safe. Today there are five, and the two most-used
   (ServerTabs, HostingTabs) use replaceState so Back exits the page and ?tab= only works on
   first render. New rule: tabs are real routes or pushState, always deep-linkable.
3. One page-shell contract. Today: 34 pages PortalHero, 4 PageHeader, 2 neither, 1 bare h1,
   1 aria-hidden void. One PageHeader primitive, one content width, one section rule.
4. The sidebar adapts to the estate. Kinds the customer owns are pinned; kinds they don't own
   collapse into "Explore" under Deploy. A one-VPS customer should not carry 21 rows.
5. The command palette becomes a real command palette: actions (deploy, add funds, restart,
   open ticket) plus the 8 entity types currently unindexed (volumes, SSL, invoices, projects,
   sites, nxcloud, migrations, free-MC).

content.text:
The sandbox is now a real portal rather than a showcase. It opens at the same URL, which lands on Home instead of the design system:

```
https://flow.k9x4rq7wpz2ah6t.nxeon.cloud/ds/home
```

The Phase 2 showcase is untouched and still at `/ds/design`.

**What was implemented.** Twenty-three routes under a new portal route group, all wrapped in one shell. The sidebar is rebuilt on the Phase 1 IA in three tiers — Create, Your resources, Account and operations — so nobody has to work out which items are products and which are account functions. Resource kinds the customer owns are pinned as children with live counts; kinds they do not own are absent from the rail entirely and surface under Deploy instead, so a one-VPS customer does not carry the same rows as an estate customer.

The active state carries four signals at once: a gradient edge marker, a raised surface, a signal-coloured icon and heavier weight. It never depends on a subtle background, and never on colour alone.

**The IA defect is fixed.** Resource kinds are now real routes, `/resources/vps/atlas-web` and `/resources/game/survival-smp`, so the URL states the kind and the nav highlight can no longer disagree with the page. In production a game server opened under "Servers" and the highlight jumped on every click. The breadcrumb reads Nxeon, Resources, VPS, atlas-web.

**The command palette leads with verbs.** Production indexed eight entity types and offered zero actions. This one indexes every resource kind, domains, mailboxes, invoices, every page and all sixteen tools, and puts actions first — searching "atlas" returns "Restart atlas-web" above the resource itself. Full keyboard navigation, Home and End, grouped results, empty and no-results states, Cmd or Ctrl K to toggle.

**Nothing was stranded.** All forty-three production destinations are mapped, every legacy `/dashboard/*` path redirects, and the mapping is visible in-app at `/ds/routes`. That includes the seven routes that had no navigation entry at all in production: NxCloud, projects, invoices, affiliate, feedback, free Minecraft and the dead order stub. Each now has a home.

**Files.** New: `lib/nav.ts` (the IA and route map), `lib/estate.ts`, `components/shell/` (PortalShell, Sidebar, TopBar, CommandPalette, PageShell, ShellStates, Inventory), and the `app/(portal)/` tree. Changed: `next.config.ts` for redirects, `app/page.tsx` now lands on Home.

**IA decisions and deviations.** Your brief's example breadcrumb said "Compute"; I used "Resources", because that is what Phase 1 approved and the prompt names Phase 1 as source of truth. SSL moved under Network and mail, since a certificate is an attribute of a domain rather than a product. The sixteen tools were demoted from a permanent sidebar row to the rail footer and the palette, since they are duplicated verbatim on the marketing site. Refer and Affiliate merged into Settings, as the audit found them to be the same code and same reward shown twice.

**Technical note.** No new issues surfaced. The build is clean, no page overflows at 1440, 768 or 390 pixels, the drawer is usable on mobile, and focus order starts at the skip link.

**Production untouched** — nxeon.cloud, pricing and login all return 200, and I made no change outside the sandbox tree. **Isolation holds** — no fetch, no environment variable, no database or payment library anywhere in the source, and the runtime dependency list is still exactly next, react and react-dom. **No product surfaces were migrated** — every product route renders a placeholder that names the capabilities Phase 1 catalogued and states that the panels arrive in a later phase.

PHASE 3 COMPLETE — NXEON APPLICATION SHELL READY FOR REVIEW

Both fixed. Refresh `/ds/deploy` to see it.

**On the grey.** My "one signal colour at a time" rule was right for actions and wrong applied to everything, which is how a nine-product catalogue ended up as nine identical boxes. Product identity is a third colour axis, separate from the action colour and the state colours, and it is information: it makes a VPS card, a VPS row and a VPS icon recognisable as the same thing at a glance.

Nine identity tokens now exist. VPS azure, game magenta, hosting cyan, domain jade, email amber, storage periwinkle, website builder spring green, NxCloud coral, free tier green. The discipline that keeps it from sliding back into decoration is one rule: identity colour may tint an icon, a hairline or a wash, but it may never become a button. Actions stay signal or brand, so the thing you click is still unambiguous.

That colour now runs through the sidebar resource icons, the inventory filter chips and row tiles, the Home metric figures, and the whole Deploy catalogue.

**On Deploy.** Rebuilt as a money page rather than a directory.

- A gradient hero using your "47 seconds" line, with the proof points beside it.
- Nine product cards, each carrying its own colour in the icon tile, the price and a top edge rule, lifting and glowing in that colour on hover.
- Plans expand inline. Clicking VPS opens four plans with the discounted rate large, the original struck through, and "then $20.99/mo" stated underneath, so renewal is never a surprise.
- A term ladder with Recommended and Best value badges, percentage-off chips, and the real saving in money: save $50.38 over one year, $302.26 over three.
- A running total pinned at the bottom of the panel: $201.50 due today, then $20.99 a month, saving $50.38 a year, next to the gradient Configure and pay button.
- A trust bar underneath.

Nothing overflows at 1440, 768 or 390 pixels. Production is untouched and the sandbox is still fully isolated.

One thing I did not do: build the actual wizards behind each product. Those are Phase 5, and this hub is the destination they consolidate into. If you want the VPS or game funnel built for real next, that is the natural follow-on.

Done. Deploy now leads with exactly those four, in that order: VPS, shared hosting, domain, game servers.

**One thing I did differently, deliberately.** Domain does not get a plan grid. The Phase 1 blueprint was explicit that a domain needs a different mental model from compute — it opens with a large "find your domain" search, and management happens after purchase, not before. So selecting Domain reveals a search field and a pricing table showing register, renew and transfer side by side. The competitor research flagged that three-column view as the single highest-trust intervention in the domain category, because renewal shock is that category's biggest trust failure. Putting a `.com` at $9.99 to register and $13.99 to renew in the same row, before anyone commits, is the whole point.

The other three keep the plan grid and term ladder, since they are priced the same way: plan plus term, with both the discounted rate and the renewal rate shown.

**Business email moved out of the headline set** and into an "Also available" row with block storage, the website builder, NxCloud and the free Minecraft tier. It is still one click from the same page. Demoting a product should never strand it, which is the same rule that gave the seven orphaned production routes a home.

The hero now reads four guided flows rather than nine products, so the count matches what is actually on offer.

Also fixed while I was in there: those secondary cards were truncating their names at five across, so the price moved onto its own line under the label.

Nothing overflows at desktop or mobile, the public URL serves it, and production is untouched.

lastPrompt: what would you call the design system if i wanted to replicate it

content.text:
Not an asset library, no. That's worth being precise about, because it changes what you'd hand someone.

**There are almost no assets in it.** No image files, no icon files, no illustration files. The sixty icons are drawn in code, the illustrations are inline SVG, the topology and the globe are generated at runtime, and the only static data file is an 11KB land bitset for the globe. Nothing to put in a folder and ship.

**What it actually is: a design system, distributed as two things.** A token layer, which is `app/globals.css` — colour, type, space, radius, elevation, motion, z-index, focus, all as CSS custom properties. And a React component library, which is `components/system/` and `components/shell/`. That's it. Porting it means copying those two directories and adding three Google fonts. No asset migration, no build pipeline.

**If you want a name**, I'd call it **Filament**. The status filament is the signature element, it's an engineering word that suits an infrastructure company, and it reads well in a sentence: "built on Filament, the Nxeon design system." Alternatives that fit the same world are Plate, Notch, or Signal, though Signal collides with the accent-colour token already named that.

**If you want someone to replicate the look from scratch**, this is the paragraph that gets you there:

> Dark navy instrument-panel interface. Layered near-black navy surfaces separated by blue-grey hairlines, never neutral grey. A blue to violet to magenta brand gradient used sparingly on the primary action and the mark. Nine product-identity hues that tint icons and edges but never become buttons. Cyan neon rationed to live states only. Objects the user owns carry a chamfered corner and a two-pixel status filament; containers do not. Technical values live on recessed monospace plates. Sections are grouped by labelled hairline rules rather than card borders. Archivo for display, IBM Plex Sans for reading, IBM Plex Mono for data. Small radii, minimal shadow, no glassmorphism, no ambient glow.

The three rules that actually keep it from drifting into generic dark SaaS are worth stating alongside it: a border means "separate object" and is spent by role, one action colour per view region, and nothing below 12px.

**The spec already exists in the repo.** `README.md` documents the eight enforced rules and the polish-pass decisions, and `globals.css` is commented with the reasoning behind each token group. If you hand those two files to another developer or another model, they have everything needed to extend it consistently.

content.text:
That's a legitimate pivot, and worth stopping for before I write another line of code. Rebuilding the visual language a second time without nailing the direction first is exactly how tokens get wasted.

Here's how I'd save tokens on this pass, specifically:

- **Get the direction approved on one small page before rebuilding anything else.** Last time I built tokens, 60 icons, ten-plus components, and nine demo pages (the globe, the deploy loaders, the game catalogue) in the same pass as the visual language. Most of that cost was demonstration surface, not the actual decision you needed to sign off on. This time: tokens plus four or five core components on one preview screen, you look at it, then I build outward only after that's right.
- **Keep what isn't actually the problem.** The Phase 3 shell, the navigation model, the routes, the command palette, the mock data — none of that is what you're reacting to. If I don't need to touch it, I won't regenerate it.
- **Fewer, larger edits instead of many small round trips.** Each rebuild-restart-screenshot cycle costs real tokens; I'll batch decisions rather than iterate one component at a time.

The current build stays at `/opt/nxeon-designsystem` untouched as a fallback, nothing is lost.

What I can't do efficiently is guess the actual direction — "flat," "too complex," and "not appealing to the average user" while also "developer-driven" is a real tension (Stripe and Railway both thread it, but land in very different places), and I don't want to spend a build cycle finding out which side you mean.

What's actually different from what I built before, tied back to your references:

- **Near-black canvas with drifting glow orbs** behind the hero — violet, magenta and cyan, blurred and layered, slowly animated. This is the ambient light every reference has and my system had none of.
- **Pill-shaped everything.** Buttons, nav, badges — full rounded rather than the small 2–6px radii before.
- **The brand gradient as a filled surface**, not a hairline. It's the primary CTA and the glowing headline text, at real saturation instead of restrained to a thin rule.
- **Glass panels**: translucent, blurred, a soft border that lifts and glows on hover rather than a flat hairline.
- **The chamfered "notch" is retired.** It fought against rounded glass, so ownership is now a soft green glow ring around the card instead — see the `atlas-web` row.
- **Product identity colour is bolder** — filled tinted icon tiles rather than a faint wash.

Three things to react to specifically:

1. Does the glow feel right, or too much / not enough?
2. Pills everywhere, or should some elements (data tables, technical panels) stay sharper for contrast?
3. Type is much bigger and bolder now — good, or overcorrected?

I've spent very little here on purpose — one CSS file, one page, no component library changes yet. Tell me what to adjust and I'll refine this one page until it's right before propagating it into the sidebar, Deploy, Home and the rest.

What changed from the last version, specifically because it's an app now and not a hero:

Two things I deliberately toned down from the marketing version, tell me if either is wrong: the display type is smaller here since a dashboard heading doesn't need hero scale, and the pill radius on rows is slightly tighter than on buttons, since a list of many rows reads better with a bit less roundness than a single CTA.

**1 · Clean light SaaS** — white, one blue accent, small radius, tight borders. Linear or Vercel territory. Most approachable to a non-technical user, least "designed."

**2 · Warm approachable** — soft off-white, coral-to-indigo gradient, generous rounding. Closer to Stripe. Friendly without losing polish.

**3 · Terminal mono** — near-black, monospace throughout, sharp corners, one green signal colour. The most explicitly developer-facing option, least "average user" friendly on its own.

**4 · Playful flat gradient** — dark base, solid violet-to-pink gradient fills, no blur or glow anywhere. Keeps colour and energy from the rejected direction without the glass or the neon.

**5 · Soft neumorphic slate** — light grey-blue, depth from dual soft shadows instead of borders, muted periwinkle accent. Calm and tactile, reads least "technical" of the six.

**6 · Bold brutalist** — white, thick black borders, sharp corners, one loud yellow block, hard offset shadow. Distinctive and structural, the option least like a template.

Point me at a number, or mix two — for instance the light warmth of 2 with the accent energy of 4 is a real combination, not just a compromise.
